Mr_DNAB Nimull,

Millinery will be somewhat costly this season, so many handsome feathers are essential to the style of a felt hat. Many hats are made entirely of velvet, and these are not turned up in front, and filled in with choux of velvet or chiffon, while plumes or aigrettes of feathers adorn the front, Handsome buckles are a leading feature of the new millinery, and although turned-up fronts in Ad- miral or Punchinello styles are conspicuously fashionable, the all-round mushroom and sailor shapes are still worn, but with soft crowns of figured velvets, or of mirroir velvet, spangled with jewels.

A fashionable . , of the new corded beaver in black, with a large rosette of beaver ribbon at the left side, caught with a paste buckle. On either side of the hat is a long black ostrich feather of beautiful quality, and the tips of these hang over the hat, and rest on the hair of the wearer. ..

On autumn coats the easy basque is equally as fashionable as the short, and the seam- across the hips in Newmarket style appears both on autumn and winter coats. Cloth coats of different colour to the skirt are in favour, the fronts rounded, backs drooping low almost to a point, and the neck with high tabbed collars or lapels turned out and edged with fur. Small velvet jackets with short basques have fussily arranged fronts, gradu- ated revers, and pouched vests, or they are double- breasted and plain, with fancy collets, almost like tiny shoulder capes, making a good medium for far or feather borders.

Of the plainer cloth coats, built on strict tailor , lines, there are a large variety; but with a good figure a light-fitting coat made with a plain ; light vest, looks well and forms a complete out door costume with a plain skirt to match. Lines of loose stitching cover the basque and out- line the coat, and the vest fastens at one of the button lines, or the opening may be in the centre if desired.

Capes are difficult to describe, but slope down long at the back, the fronts rounded, and so uni- versal are circular or bias frills that these appear even on the old golf cape' and are duplicated several times on evening cloaks or smart capes, the frills tapering off quite narrow in front. The very short circular cape appears with long, pointed fronts, glorified by folded revers and cascades of frills in pleated silk or other material. For matronly figures there is a revival in dolman form, but with wider sleeves, which do not confine the arms; and the rounded capes are also appropriate when supplemented by stole ends falling beneath the frilled fronts.

The newest skirts for cloth and woollen fib th• hips like a sheath, and are cut in three parts only. (the back folds over in deep, flat pleats meeting in the centre, and these fasten with buttons or tabs, and train slightly at the back. Evening skirts for dinners and ceremonious occasions have quite trained backs, but the dance gown rests well on the ground without actually trailing, and the width is increased by ruches and fussy trimmings. Mantles with indefinite points back and front (says The Lady), have openings for the arms, and are bordered with fur, and completed by fur- trimmed collets, and are especially becoming to middle-aged wearers. 'Skirts are more elaborate than ever, and, the perfectly plain skirt is voted old, although many fashionable women have the courage to wear it without a separate foundation. Gored and shaped flounces prevail, and overskirts are rapidly becoming acclimatised. Sometimes the flounced skirt has each part lined separately, as, for instance, the flounce lined flat, and the top With its own distinct lining„ but many fanciful skirts have a plain gored foundation, which fits the upper part all but the extra tfflness at the edge. Smock dresses are still all but universal for children under six or seven, but there is one pretty new style which is shaped slightly to the figure by means of perpendicular tuckings at the waist. Big collars of spotted and embroidered muslin, edged with frills, are fashionable with nearly all frocks, and many are turned back in front to show a frnall V-shaped chemisette of the same fabric as the collar. As to colours, every shade of grey, mahogany, claret, Havana brown, and dull blue, seem to be the most in favour, although scarcely any tint can be said to bo absolutely out of fashion.

The Eton-fronted bodice for young girls is not yet out of favour, though a newer and very pretty shape has straight fronts drawn in at the waist, but opening rather widely above to show a smart vest of embroidered muslin, tucked silk, or braided face cloth. Sometimes the loose fronts are closely striped with rows of velvet or ribbon, and when this is the case the skirt as well as the top of the sleeves correspond as to trimming. Older girls— i.e., from 11 to 16—will wear basqued bodices this season, and the Norfolk shape is popular in but. it wanamatsis careful ortlinagthdiree.sbsrmeaaskteerd. tweed antod sculiotthurrrlncE:i cutting successfully turned out by Girls of all ages adopt the shot,. 'moque coat for outd,Jors, and if it is not a very graceful garment it is at any rate a thoroughly comfortable one. Your loving Jsas

div.head: "CAPITAL" CHAT.
div.p: "CAPITAL" CHAT.

The attempt to blackmail the Dean of Norwich by threatening to publish his biography reminds me of a characteristic saying of Mr. Gladstone's. When Mr. George Russell was asked to write a monograph of Mr. Gladstone in the series of" The Queen's Prime Ministers " he applied to Mr. Glad- steno for his consent and some assistance in the work. Mr. Gladstone replied," I will not do what Bishop Phillpotts did, who brought an injunction in Chancery to prevent a man from writing his life and that is all the help that I can give you."

Professor E. Ray, Lankaster, the new director of the Natural History Museum, will commence his duties there and take over from Sir W. Flower the charge of the collections in the course of next week The existing arrangements as regard the division of the department of zoology into three separate sections, with an assistant keeper at the head of each, will, it is understood, be maintained, and in other respects the working and organisation of the establishment will in no way be disturbed, notwith- standing reports to the contrary current in scienti- fic circles a short time back.

Another of the interim reports of the Committee on Dangerous Trades, which under the presidency of Mr. Tennant, M.P., has done such valuable work, has been issued. It deals with the file cutting, gal- vanised iron work, glass-polisbing, the manufacture and use of grindstones, and other industries. Gal- vanised iron works in London, Birmingham, Glas- gow,Liverpool, and elsewhere were visited by the Committee, evidence being taken from the em- ployers and workmen. This evidence does not lead the Committee to believe that serioes consequences ensue from the inhalation of the mixture of gases and vapours generated in the galvanising process. But while they do not consider this an industry which should be scheduled as a dangerous trade, and are consequently not prepared to recommend special rules for its control, they suggest the wide- spread introduction of mechanical fans for ridding workshops of part of the fumes, and they do ntt consider that work in a galvanising shop is good for young and growing boys and girls.

The friction which has arisen at Battersea be- tween the costermongers and the tradesmen is by no means the first case of its kind in the metropolis, and I am wondering whether it will end as others have ended. The tradesmen in a certain part of London complained of the casters, and by setting the police in motion succeeded in getting them re- move 1. The mime 'late result was that their own trade fell off, and after a while they actually ar- ranged to have the stalls back again. So it has been in other parts of the town. The truth is that the stalls assist in bringing a crowd together, and that people who purchase at the stalls frequently buy at the shops as well. As to the stories of very large incomes,say £6OO or .£BOO a year,being earned b,y costermongers, such cases must be very rare. though I have seen a very fine fish stall in one of the North London streets,the owner of which is re- ported to make at least £3OO a year, and close by the keeper of a flower stall stands only two days a week, and lives comfortably out of the proceeds.

I understand that the delay which has taken place in the publication of the official report on the outrages to which Mr. Savage Landor was subjected by the Thibetans was due to the unwillingness of the India Office to allow the document, to be made public. Now, a year after the report was written and more than a year after the outrageous treat- ment to which Mr. Lander was subjected, there is less danger that an outcry may be raised for the punishment of the men who were responsible for the inhuman cruelties inflicted on Mr. Landor and his servants, Mr. Landor was in the poasession of the Chinese passports, but it may be assumed that these gave him no authority to attempt to reach Lhassi ; and travellers who enter Thibet with the intention of visiting the mysterious capital know that they run great risks and must take their chance of being turned back and even subjected to insult and il:-•reattnent. But it is not pleasant to think that a British eubjecr, was treated as Mr. Landor was treated without some attempt being made to bring the guilty persons to book; and it was, I believe.because the Indian authorities feared that public opinion might impose on them some ' such duty that they have delayed so long the pub- lication of the official confirmation of Mr. Savage Lan does try.

One of the morning'papers came out to-day with a placard hearing th 3 words "De Rougenaont Ex- posed." The phrase wee not intended ta apply to the ~oene at St. Jrfties'ii'Hall when M. de Rouge- moot stood on the platform, with arms bared to the shoulder, defying his critics todetect a penal brand. It is anether kind of exposure that the modern Cru.ios's journalistic tormentor hoe in view. lie alleges that M. de Itougemont is identical with a person named Grien, who was trying to snake a liv- ing a few weeks ago as the inventor of a diving hell, or alternately as an artist in black and white. The story, even were it provad to be true, would probably not greatly disconcert M. de Rougemont. He i the coolest, frankest, moat cynical of men. "Yes," he might say in the vein of much of his lec- ture of last night. "I have had my wits sharpened by adversity, and that was one of my exvldienta to earn a little bread." A popular audience finds that kind of thing not unpleasing. Thus the feeling of the St. James's Hall audience saemed lobe that de Rougemont must be speaking i the truth, else he would never dare to n flagrantdulge in the cynicisras of which be appears to be so fond.

It is now said that the negotiations with t ranee about Fashoda are to begin at once, though this is contradicted by other reports. But the latest news gces to show that Siarchand's position is quite un- tenable, and that by this time his force Would have been annihilated but for the victory of Omdurman, If the reinforcements which were aaid to have been despatched to him ten days ago have really set out, they will Rot reach him before the beginning of ' next year, by which time Lord Salisbury should have brought the Fasheda question to a close. Fortunately the French Government appears to be more reasonable than the French press. But sup- posing the reinforcements arrived in the neighbour- hoon of Fashoda before diplomacy was done with the question, they would not be allowed to enter Fashoda. Perhaps the Gocdion knot may yet be cut by Marchand's Soudanese deserting him it,* service in the Egyptian army, where they will get better pay and bettor food. Some have already abandoned him. It may be cut by Marchand being starved out of his peit ion, for if he claims Fashoua, he has no cltdm to the country round, to which he must look for supplies. His little continent is in the position of a bessiged garri,on, unless the clemency of his enemy sends him suppliee. Thus it is clear Francs cannot play the Niger game of procrastination over again; for, while negotiaton are talking in Paris or London, events are in-vitably marching on to a sllution of the problem at Fashoda itself.

I learn that Mr. It L. Jefferson, who set out amid the sound of a good many cycling trumpets 6003.0 weeks ago, to ride to Khiva, in Central Asia, on his bicycle has reached his destination in a broken- down condition. He is quite unable to ride back, and will perform the desert part of the journey on the back of a camel, and the rest by the Trans- Caspian arid other railways. Fever, dysentery, starvation, and sleeping in the open-air, with the danger of being stung almost to death by scorpions or devoured by tigers, he arrived at Khiva a perfect wreck in the beginning of September, and I do not know if the state of his hsalth permits of hi even yet setting out on his homeward journey. The experiences of Mr. Fo4ter Fraser and his friends were mere child's play compared with Mr. Jeffer— sou's, and he will have a stirring book to write when be C.31.22t9 home.

—„ Gratitude (a London newspaper avers) is becoming one of the rarest of virtues. But we often fird evidence that it is not yet extinct. A " Sheffield Weekly lade- pendent " reporter writes I lately investigated some circumstances which contrsdict cynics who acsert that people fe rget favours received. I was commissioned to call upon Miss Helen A. Foster, of 1.08, South View-road, Sheffield, in consequence of the receipt of a Ptter from from that lady which vas rec iced by a prininent business house, as follows :—" I scarcely knew how In thank you for the benefit which you have given me." There is no necessity to reproduce the whole !iotal. ; it was rent without s Alcitation or suggestion, and was full of expressions el gratitoe. Misa Foster was at home, and evidently occupied a comfertab'e position in life. I complimented her on looking so well and cheerful, wh,in the lady rromntly replied : "Yes, hut if you had seen me a few months ago you would have been sympathising with me." " I learn from your letter that you have had a re- markable recovery from a very serious illness. Will you kindly relate the circumstances ?" " Certainly. In the first place I will say I enjoyed ex- cellent health until thres years ago. Teen I began to suffer from indig,estion, which gradually locoman chronic, brouht on other maladiv, anFl made me a mere wreck." "Will von describe some of the symptoms? " "Yes; I could rot possibly have been were. I lost my appetite completely.and became reduced to skin and bone. I was always fired, even whea I need no exer- tion,as much so in the morning after I had just got oP : as I was at night."

"Were you able to sleep ?" "I obtained some Weep, hut it never seemed to refroh me. I also bad pains all over me. I seas af.aid to it dawn for five minutes, because I knew when I tried to rise again a sharp pain would pass through me, as if had strained myself ; and when I did sit it was always in a doubled-up position, because that was the only way I could get ease. For months I was utterly wre'chPd and miserable, and made everybody in the house sc, ag well. They used to say I wns neither useful nor orna- mental.' "

"And now you are bnth." " At any rate I am of am, because I noir do a dales wotk with anybody. As to being an ornament I can Sax that I am not the apectacle I used to be." "Did you ever think your life vrqs in danger ?" " Oh, I quite gave myself ue as lost. So would anY- one else who got as low as I did." t. What steps did you take ti effect a cure ?" " I called in no less thin four dnetots,but they neither did me any apparent good nor told me what was the matter with me. They all sail I had indigestion of some kind,hut that ia all. Then I trind a ehange of air. The sea-side not suiting me. I silent a whole month in the country, but I came hack just as bad as when I went. I elan tried all sort aof pills and medicines which I saw advert land."

" Now, please tell me of your cure." " I read la the paners of eeveral persons, whrt`io symptoms were similar to my own. being cured by taking Dr. Williams' Pink Pills for Paig Peopla. A ith'itigh I had lost all hope of recovery, and all fait h in 111 f dielpfP. I determined to give them a trial. They proved just what was wanted, and as my strength began to return I persevered with them. After three boxes I mended rapidly, and now I feel stronger and better than I have done for rears. Nobody enjors life better. I have no need of medicine now, but I 'always keep some of Dr. Williams' Pink Pills for Pale Poop'e in the house ; but I have never stiff, red a relapse." div.head: EXAMINER FRIDAY, OCTOBER 7 1898
div.p: THE EXAMINER FRIDAY, OCTOBER 7 1898
uked, vary callously: is lark now on grua arms we this Muro, his rival?" __ . - . _

, Puke looked at me with a broad grin. "I'm tosh classed ef I know. Mark Pepys bein' genTman born an' bred—" A troublesome tooth cut the sentence short. "How'd ye ken that ? " "Whoa, Sandy!" exclaimed Puke. "Leastways I guess he's a genTman, by his standin' among the landed gentry of these parts." "I've often wondered whether he hails free

beyond the border." "Hey ye now?" smilingly answered the tavern- keeper. "So hey I; but not bein' sorter keen on his pedigree, I dunno. All fish is fish to me, an' the arnalrns is choice." He nodded to me good-temperedly and winked; F 0 I remarked: "That's verra kindly put, liar;* I notice a peculiar device tattooed on Mark's az "Tattooed!" laughingly exclaimed the lan& lord, incredulity expressive on his face. "Why I've taken thet to be a birth-mark. I'm blest ef ye don't jest about notice things. I'll hey a good look next time." And smartly turning the subject, he added: "I ain't a cove ez deals in personalities. My customers want to hear ef our union wi' the American States will be confirmed. Politics is pow'ful wi' the men, an' I'm sick to see our women mad on the craze, an' losin' thar,gen'l'ness in consequence. Depend on it, Sandy, ef our mothers an' daughters dabble in politics, home comfort'll suffer, an they'll lose ther influence over our boys' an' gals." "Pecos tells me that Queen Kane o' Golden Vale has 'blue stockings ' to assist i' the counsels o' her tribe." "Pecos talks at random. Put his words through a sieve."

This was candid, and irritating, because foreign to my purpose. "Wee!, Harry, I can understand pretty wumen, like Lucia Diaz, sittin' on committees, fer wi' susceptible men beauty's will is law. Tak' a case. If Lucia wished to see London, Mark wouldna scruple to tak' her. He'd be richt proud to show sic a beauty i' fashionable London." "Ef thar's a corner o' the globe whar Mark wouldn't care to go, it's England." "Wherefore ?" "'Cause his money is in stock an' land here," replied Puke, perceiving the drift of my question. No better reason, an' fer no other, ez I know." "I'd like to hae a bet wi' ye on't." "Ef I took ye, Sandy, I reckon it'd be daylight robbery," answered Puke with a tantalising grin, "an' I'm not hungry enough to suck a skewer." I laughed heartily, and said: "Om I wouldna say that Mark willna get hamesick. A Scotchman migratt j to stop." "An', cuckoo-like," sarcastically replied the merry tavern-keepeer,"to turn the aborigines out o' ther own nest." "I suppose ye ken o Mark's early associations?" "To tell the honest truth, Sandy, I never trouble whar my customers spring from, so long ez they pay ther score. Thet's business." I accepted the well-deserved snub, and admired Puke's disposition. "By the bye, Sandy I've carried out yer wishes, an' arranged for ye to see the Indian wolf-dance on the heights. Nme o' the braves seem to hey washed since ther birth." "A leetle o' yer ` soft soap ' wonldna come amiss." But the happy-go-lucky dunderhead appar- ently failed to grasp my meaning. "Ony squaws an' kids ? " "No. By the condition o' titer ponies' unshod aoofs, an' the way they eagerly barter ther fishin' tackle an' wicker baskets, I should say they've seen rough travellin'. I had to drive a hard bar- gain, fer the wretches would cheat a Whitechape, Jew—though the pore devils are harmless as doves."

_ After approving the negotiations, I determined at once to embrace the opportunity of seeing a bit of Indian rough-and-tumble life; and mounting my sure-footed mustang, I was soon trotting at a brisk

pace towards .the encampment. Strange that I should notice this ; but just to my left, within a small, undulating field, were two oxen yoked to a harrow composed of branches. The shabby half- caste who tended them was watching a bit of beef and some frijoles frying in a pan over a charcoal fire, while he was patting a maize tortilla with his hands, ready for baking between heated sheets of iron. In this characteristic gipsy fashion the herdsman lived, his bill of fare occasionally varied by the substitution of weak chocolate, rice, boiled onions, red pepper, and such fruits as he could conveniently beg or steal. I halted to admire the rich showing of flowers which literally covered the hills. And as I gazed with wonder and delight upon this picture so ineffably fine, my mind was awakened to the sterner things of life by the evensong of the red- men. My pony instinctively wheeled round towards the spot from whence the chanting came, and without the slightest hesitation I trotted into the Indian camp receiving that hearty reception which is given an expected and honoured guest. Harry Puke had evidently turned his kindly disposition and glib tongue to good account, for the hospitality of these redmen was both demonstrative and generous. Possibly a knowledge that I carried a goodly supply of tobacco and dollars with me, as a reward for their friendliness, was some part of the incentive which procured me such an effusive welcome. Mine host, fantastically attired, his face daubed with ochre devices, and his matted hair falling about his brows and ears, sat upon a log in his dingy tent. Three ugly young men, absolutely naked, sat cross-legged around a small earthenware pot, in which was a deadly poison extracted from berries. The trio ceased tipping their arrows with the poison, and one of them tethered my pony, and gave it hay. What little shelter the braves had was simply formed of boughs set up like a pyramid of muskets, and covered with rags, leaves and twigs.

"The men dig outside for the wolf-dance," the chief presently observed in the simplest Spanish, replenishing his carved pipe. "In the meantime let us drink." Thereupon he picked up a short whip, to the thong of which hung a smooth oval stone, and lustily beat a tambourine, made pretty with ochre and eagles' feathers. An attendant entered, and having received instructions he ran out and soon returned with two horn cups and a jar with a short thin neck. The chief beckoned the man to fill my cup, and then he held his own for the liquid. To assure me of good faith, he tossed off his drink and asked for more; so I could not offend one so kindly disposed, and followed suit. The stuff was not objectionable, tasting something like lager beer; and when he smacked his lips with relish, I smiled. As darkness had set in, we strolled out, and the chief gave a whoop. Shortly the camp was as busy as an ant-hill. Warriors pulled the skins from the chief's tent and clothed themselves, others lit a fire, and by the time the hylas were making their delightfully clear and tranquil music, I was again—pardon the hackneyed phrase—"cementing our friendship." Good luck to the Indian cup that cheers the senses and gives wonderful elasticity to the step! The warriors threw themselves on all fours, and imitated wolves by scratching and sniffing the earth. Then they centred to a spot near us, and I could plainly see them tear up a live Indian—one previously and lightly interred. Then there wi • great rejoicing and dumb motions, succeeded by low moaning and chanting, as the "wolves" per- formed strange evolutions about the fire and the mock grave. The chief grinned, and cast sly glances at me, for I was in that merry mood which paints the devil a saint. And yet, in my fancy, I heard Pecos calling afar off: ."Sandy, Sandy, where art thou, maudlin fool!" I laughed with derision; and the orgies went on apace. Now I confess to feeling somewhat suspicious during the finale, for my whole being was exhilarated, and then objects vanished as a strange drowsiness gradually numbed eve,-,, sense in me. 'then with a malicious ho#' the chief sprang upon me from behind, and con- certed action against me proved how the rascals had connived at my capture. Some disarmed me, others tied my arms and legs, and the chief rogue and prime mover gagged me in a trice. Great beads of perspiration broke out on my forehead, - the cords pressed deep into my flesh as I struggled in vain, and in my frenzy I tried to curse Puke, whose presents had suborned these fiends to covet a ransom. "Cease your struggles, or I slit your jugular vein!" hissed the chief, pointing the blade of his knife at my throat. So fearful was my dread of torture, that I suddenly jerked my head • but the wily sinner anticipated my intention, and sheathed ' the weapon. My wrists were bound behind my back, and lashed to my feet. The extremely pleasant sensation, as though dogs gnawed the small of my back, resulted. I saw men heaping dried grass and twigs near the fire, and I shud- dered as the significance of this dawned upon my sobered mind. "My God!" I thought, "I'm to be roasted alive on a spit!" The gloating rascals fed the fire, and then the chief placed a pair of large pincers among the hot I embers. I closed my burning lids, for at the sight —regale

of this my e 3 b sr,tutst as tootign tney would start from their st :kris. My brain was on fire, every square incl if my skin crept, the veins of my forehead stii out, my tongue and lips Were parched witb theit, streams 'of agony-sweat ran down .1 T was doomed to the slow torture of having my flesh singed with lighted oil-rags! I could see all the preparations for my. linger- ing death; and when a high stake was driven in at either side of the roaring fire, and a pole tied across for suspending my. .body over the flames, a cold, clammy feeling stole Over me. I felt deathly sick, and shuddered and groaned in an agony of despair. Thereupon a vicious monster seized a clod of mud, and slung it at my head, striking me abaft the left ear with a force which half stunned me. The chief evidently wanted such sport reserved for himself, for he swore at and kicked the miscreant; afterwards dancing around me with delight, and mocking me as the "wolves "howled for permission to begin their gruesome task. "A fool always bathes above the rapids," hissed the chief in my ear. Then he made a sign, and the Indians struck camp speedily, for a contingent had galloped in from Yerba Buena. All mounted and hastened northward, leaving the chief alone to hack, hew, and frizzle me to death, or to prolong my agonies as the brutal whim pleased him. The grinning villain deliberately bared my breast, then lit an oiled rag, and brought it upon the red- dot pincers. In his right hand he held his bowie knife. My body shivered convulsively as the steel glittered in the fire glow. I closed my eyes as the knife descended—not to Maim, but to sever tlitio bonds around my legs. But my wrists were still tied behind me, and the gag-was in my mouth. "When next you insult a Castilian," he said with a sarcastic grin, "you shall be tall;ed, feathered, and burnt upon the hill-top as a warn- ing to Mark Pepys 1" With which unexpected threat he leaped to his horse, and laughing heartily, galloped away into pitch darkness. That chief was blurt)!
CHAPTER IV. TRE ROUSING OP MARK .PEPYR.

I fainted, and on recovering consciousness found Mark saturating my hair and bathing my temples with water. Lucia Diaz held a lighted lantern, and Puke's :scared face appeared uncanny in the glare. He was kneading my limbs like a master of massage. A thousand stars danced before m. 7 blood-shot eyes. I shivered as one stricken with ague. I moaned an explanation, but Mark laughed my "Muro yarn " to scorn, imagining I had dreamt it. He said that the Indians had strapped Puke down his own cellar, and turned the tavern topsY- turvy. Half-dazed, I gasped: "Hoot, man! I'm no' a doited "The knaves have stolen everything precious and portable," added Mark, "stimulating their thievery by clearing out Puke's stock at one fell swoop. An agonised sigh was my response, and struggling to my feet, I :.hoarsely muttered: "My stupeedity exemplifies the auld sayin' : 'Pules rush in whar angels fear to tread.' I'll gang awa an' droon wysel " "You are too tottery on your pins, old fellow," observed Mark, good-temperedly, "and the comi- cality of your admission under such distressing circumstances tickles even poor Puke." "If the blackguards drunk his whiskey," said I, tantalised beyond endurance, "half are corpses, fer Puke sold vile stuff."

Ye prefer neat pulque," Puke retorted, "palatable, but strong enough to play skittles wi' a red-haired Scotchman. Our patient gets cross; a sure sign he's on the mend!" Lucia's commiseration amounted to a reminder that I looked like a half-drowned rat. Just my luck—humbled again before this woman! ShorAy a scout came galloping up with excited Jip. He reported that, whoever were the prime movers, Queen Bans's warriors had received Mark's 'treasures, and were now miles up the river on their way to Golden Vale. Puke stamped his foot with rage, and paced to and fro like one crazed. "I'm ruined I" he cried. "Pecos is m.issin . He's an accomplice, an' ez gone off we the curse him!" Mark and Lucia were itte-d-tete, but they turned. Por a moment I held my breath in astonishment, arid stared at Lucia Diaz, firmly pressing my lips. Her white fase glimmered in the rays of the lantern, but no gesture nor tremour betrayed her thoughts. "They've stolen my telescope, knife an' pistol," said lat length. "The pistol has S.D.' on the haft, that may be a clue." Puke pricked his ears, and I pointedly added: "We must track doon the mean an' cowardly red- skins, wha hadna the courage to be warlike, nor the friendliness to keep faith durin' peace. But I winna believe that Pecos was a traitor."

An angry gust of wind came up from the restless sea as Puke observed: "Never trust a crook-back. Deviltry kern ez nat' ral to Pecos ez a silver pine to a Chipmunk. He covorted about my place ez ef in league wi' the Indians." "People speak ill of him only because he's con- scious of his affliction," said Mark, as he stopped the plague of Jip's strange dumb solicitude. "No back-biting, Puke, no vilifying an absent man." We walked along in that awkward silence which made me wonder what sort of calamity would break it. Jip limped on a foreleg, and sniffed and growled in a churlish manner. He caressed Lucia and pawed his master's knees. He whined when the wind whistled through the trees, and he had to be cuffed and held by the ears before we could safely cross Puke's threshold. "Oot on omens!" said L "but the sagacious brute smells blood." And Mark laughed and the dog whined simultaneously. Without raising my eyebrows I glanced up at Lucia. Her beautiful dark eyes were watching me intently. To my sober mind Mark's love-making appeared somewhat too risque; for although this worry was paramount yet he found time and the necessary sentiment to be gulled by Lucia's beauty and chicanery. A strong man in leading strings is always a sorry sight. The Senorita knew that I suspected her of craft, and the more morose Mark's worship made my disposition the more studied was her civility. I tried to take the sublime conceit out of her by throwing cold water on her hero's passionate love, but the fiery brilliancy of her full dark eyes electrified him. Imagine my profound disgust, therefore, when Mark went a-courting on this very night, as though, like an officer, he con- templated leaving for a foreign station on the- morrow. While we got the saloon ship-shape he. left, with his arm about her slender waist, ostensi- bly to escort her home. While we examined the, whilom treasure-room Lucia was worming her way into a :susceptible heart; while Pecos might be lingering in misery the charming Spanish gentle- woman was gracefully complimenting the man she duped. While we scolded Jip into decent behaviour, she yes, no doubt, pouring her adula- tions into Mark's willing ears, making him effemi- nate and unfit for the sterner duties of life. Here was a handsome, full-blooded man drawn like steel by the magnetic influence of this woman—as an ancient mariner enticed to destruction by the sweet music of a siren. Oh, that I had the power to blow a sirocco between them! Mark returned with a flushed face, but with set jaws and an expression of determination about his mouth. Here was the sterner half of his dual nature—an explanation of the commercial "screw" lavishly endowing his chapel—of the old warrior and recipient of a Victoria Cross breaking his heart over the grave of his daughter, of the pig-headed and ill-tempered navvy moved by Faith to good works and soul-stirring prayer. I asked myself : "Is na Lucia's cunning hid under a mask? Or is she a mere frivolous woman, unable to revoke the edicts o' the past, an' honestly loving my friend, Mark Pepys ? " My thoughts, which then went off at a tangent, were recalled by the deep, rich tones of a familiar voice: "Sandy, light a couple of dips in the parlour." And, glancing at the drowsy Puke, Mark added: "What, Harry, going to bed? Yea would drop asleep pegged to a clothes-line!" "I'm upset," returned the easy-going tavern- keeper. "Ye see my stock's not insured, an' I can t realise sufficient money to lay in even ordinary supplies fer a week. I'm at my wits' end fer a way out of the difficulty." ,‘l'm going to San Lone," said Mark, good turedly, "and I'll send you a stock right away. me when and how you can." "Thanks fer yer kindness," mumbled Puke, rubbing his eyes and yawning. "I hopes ez how ye'll find the rascals ez ransacked this yer place. First an' foremost them ez give the red-skins the plan of this house, deserve five dozen wi' the rope's end afore they're lynched." "Queen liana courts the thong," said Mark sternly, irritably knocking his leg with the handle of his whip. "She shall have something smarter." "Hang 111uro to the top-mast of yon schooner in the offing—when you catch him red-handed," onoth

ruire angrily, "and give recos the tails." 1 "Prejudice al'ays runs amuck o' argument," I lsneered at the landlord as he went to bed • and turning to Mark I asked, confidentially, whether the Senorita knew of the worth of his treasures. He winced and frowned. "So far as I know she

..„ was entirely ignorant of their existence, though Mum may have gathered that I was waiting to ship some valuable goods. In spite of my reproof elle still deigns to smile upon that regal-looking ambassador of the invisible world; so draw what inference you like. The Golden Vale holds mY goods, and ICana shall be humbled in the duet at my feet. I refuse to be influenced by your ungallant innuendo. Lucia Diaz was net an accomplice, either before or after the fact. I'm fond of the girl. I like her chic, and she dresses with taste and judgment . . . Am I not my own master ?"

_ . "I'm nat'rally ane o' the critical kind, an' I compliment ye on yer judgment o' beauty." "You gracefully climb down, Bandy. If Queen Kana's handsome daughter Olive, with all her grace and great wealth, were offered to me as a free gift, I should prefer Lucia Diaz; which, by the way, reminds me that we found footprints near Lucia's tent, square toes and pelted heels." I .quaked within, and slyly placed my soles , wider the chair. ' The wind whistled through the keyhole and moaned down the chimney; the boards creaked and Jip whined. I placed my finger upon my closed lips and listened. An agreeable lull ensued. We heard the bluster of Puke, who usually ended the day with. a comic song, but his aches and anxieties ;to-night completely stultified comedy. Ashamed of yielding to my fears I closed the door, and Mark made Jip lie on the mat; but neither master nor dog could rest; the one paced the room dejectedly, and the brute refused to be soothed.

Now it was a silent but mutual understanding between us that time should not be wasted in vain regrets concerning the treasures, and, after we were wearied out with fatigue and conjectures, I bid Mark good-night, and lay down with my clothes on, and a brace of pistols under my pillow in case of an emergency. Sleep bad hardly embrace& my weary mind when I heard Jip scratching at Mark's door and howling furiously. Then came Harry Puke's stentorian voice:
"Suthin's the matter wi the dog. A feller can't get a wink o' sleep wi' thet confounded row."

"What must it be for me?" retorted Mark. "I can't aPPere him. He'll have a sound thrashing presently. This threat uttered, I offered to shut him in the outhouse. Mark agreed, and lighting a lantern I put Jip's collar on and tied a piece of rope to it. The animal's delight knew no bounds; but when my intentions were seen, he tugged furiously to pull me away from the tavern. I secured him in the outhouse, and went indoors again; but Jip's sagacity prevailed, and his dismal barking at last convinced us weary listeners that we were stifling instincts which should be encouraged. ' "We're snubbing the brute's nature out of him," I deploringly observed. "My joints ache, but I'rn game to follow his lead."- "Then heel yourself, Sandy. We may have tough work." "Shall Puke join us ? " "No," firmly replied Mark, "he has already ha the life nearly frightened. ou,t of him. But we'll knock up some of the sturdiest lads." "Harry," I cried at Puke's door, " VVP gang whaur Jip leads. The dog scents meeschief. Bolt the front door a'ter us." "Thet hound would do fer the London detective department," sneered Puke on opening his door. "He's a darned sight too smart fer these 'ere parts. If I were young, Mark, I'd take him over; He'd be worth a thousand, an' dirt cheap at thet. The colour had fled from Mark's face before he
replied good-tern-peTialy-,--``Yo-u-;e-a-iu-nnrifeilort Harry. I shall have better use for him here; that is, if the culprits don't pick him off with a sly bullet—or me."

"Git along wi' ye, coons. None but madmeo would hunt fer seals in a minnow-pond. After recent experiences, I don't like bein' left alone; but I'm no coward. In case ye hey to knock nle up, give a password=Oxford-Don." Mark started at the significance of the word; but the landlord fussed abofit and passed it off with hearty laugh. With kindly consideration he held his lantern from the side window to light our path. I was convinced that this man knew the nature of Mark's life-stain. Jip frisked about .s.nd careseed Us, shortly "61311 along the uneven earth with such earnestness o purpose that our curiosity was rs,ite to the highest pitch. The exercise set my body in a glow, and I clenched my teeth with a firm resolve to follow w4ithersoever we were led. We pressed on straight across the uneven surface of a field, when suddenly Jip sprang forward, and having satisfied himself of an important find, set up a triumphant bark. Just as we were within measurable distance of 6 discovery our light was blown out. It seemed es , though, the evil wind had come from the nostrils „ of Lucifer hiaisielf, that Muro might draw a red herring across the scent. The light rekindled, we peered about , verY cautiously. "Sandy," exclaimed Mark, "look. there's Pecos stretched in the gully!" My heart seemed to leap into 'my-throat as I rushed a step 9f, two forward, and stared at the prostrate form. -11' was the dead body of the half-caste tiller of the soil whom I had seen cooking his meat that very after ncon.. "Stabbed to the heart!" I cried. "Some ot Pecos's beads grasped by his stiff fingers—see' a piece o' singlet—an' the bone charm that Pecos wore, carved in Golden Vale characters. Jip inlet ha' seen the murder. 0, that the dumb covld speak! A foul an' bloody wark lies on some bltte heart! " Mark involuntarily shivered the sight Ices enough to make a Mummy shudder with dread. ' We obtained the necessary assistance, for e thorough examination of the murdered man, and ' then ordered his decent burial. By the time the dawn of day made Mount Diablo and the Costa Hills stand out upon the grey light of the eastern sky, Mark and I were wending onr way to Puke's Delight. As we heard the first chirp of the birds the wind gradually abated, sot a gentler breeze came in the most delightful melodY, through the pines. The conifer kings were vivo with the hum of insects, the buzz of bees, and the songs of a thousand species of birds. The foothill° were a paradise of flowers, and as the welcome 00 began to tip the crags and crowns of the coast range with a rosy light, the air grew balmy and the scene delightful. "I take my solemn oath." Mark said, doffing hat, his eyes flashing, and his features stern Wit. uncommon , uncommon resolution, "that I will not rest till t.n mystery is cleared up, the actual thieves discovere' I and punished, and the murderer of this half-caste 4 brought to justice. By hook or by crook that she j wolf, Kana, shall he my prisoner till every ge° and jewel of mine is restored!" To dissuade him was like trying to stop the Nevada Fall with a chip cast abreast the streare•ci A big order, this, which perhaps meant ge° money thrown after ba' d • though an easy conscience is better than gold. Perhaps in seeking to avenget; he might himself discover how hard it is to exPie in. Mark explained his plans, and in the whole o,f my past experience of him he had shewn no 0r

approach to that aggressive spirit which o'o stimulated him to action. But he had never bee, so ruthlessly robbed before, no had I the* great faith in Destiny. (To. b. contistsed.) STARTLING EVIDENCE.

She had kidney diseale very badly, Ttliclt able to pass only very little water, and otteaa qutt,eseed with brick-dust. She cried out with pain, ~he ory_ tor both night and day. She had pains like a dagger 114,, vo back, her tongue was badly coated, and she WA , appetite. She has been doctoring for years, lont_7oo. no use. SYNOPSIS OF PRECEDING CHAPTERS: This story is related by Sandie Dees, a Californian trader before the days of the gold rush. His em. ployer, Mark Pepys, is in love with a Mexican girl. Lucia Diaz. Manuel Muro, a Mexican, also appears to love the girl, and Dees fears that he is plotting to take Pepys's life. He doubts the girl's good faith also.

div.head: CHAPTER 111. A LAMB AMONG WOLVES.
div.p: CHAPTER 111. A LAMB AMONG WOLVES.

For obvious reasons I kept my own counsel. The second day of the Easter festivities was a memorable one in my history. We were lolling upon the shore in the forenoon when Mark con- fided to me that Lucia Diaz wanted him to take her to the Presidio dance. Now, although Muro had apparently stocked his schooner with provisions, and was preparing to weigh anchor, yet I doubted the sincerity of Lucia's promise of silence. "The Castilian unfurls his sails," observed Mark. "The store-room is safe? "
" Yea, " I replied, somewhat coldly, "the packages are safe enough. Harry Puke is no' o' a prying nature."

"Besides," Mark added, with a reassuring air, "if he guessed the value of the articles he has the good sense to hold his tongue." I winked, and it almost seemed as though the Senorita comprehended, for a smile played about her lips as she turned her face to the sun-glow. I raised my eyebrows, and, turning aside, croaked a warning which Mark understood. "She has more delicacy of feeling, Sandy, than , you can , appreciate. , See, she strolls beyond ear-shot."

I eyed her askance and said curtly: "Mark, arc you well heeled? " He touched his repeater case, observing signifi- cantly : "Well armed, well feared." Then placing his hands on my shoulders he looked straight into my steel-Frey eyes. "You are melancholy," he said, or anxious about my safety. Well, I admire a true and faithful friend, but there is nothing to fear. You shake your head. Then cast lots, Indian fashion."

"Agreed," I answered, somewhat bitterly, placing two pieces of wood in my hat, and holding it hopefully above my head, as Lucia approached. "Long twig, Lucia wine," said he cheerfully, at which the Senorita smiled and showed her pearly teeth. Her face was lit with mingled surprise and curiosity as Mark cast his brown eyes skyward, tossed his head as though highly amused, and then with a flourish drew—the long twig! I pulled a wry face as his eyes twinkled exultantly. "Juist my luck," I growled. "I ne'er won a raffle or a draw in my life." "Don't look so glum, old chap. I enjoy a dance, while you prefer to mope like a jilted gillie. I declare, you look like a cross-grained money.. grub. There, man, go and wash down Harry Puke's yarns with some of his vile whiskey." "Bahl" I retorted disdainfully, as Lucia opened her eyes in wonder. "What's the secret o' Puke's influence o'er ye, that ye mak' his tavern yer bondin' store? ' Mark frowned and stood as stiff as a ramrod, curtly replying: "That's my business." A dark shadow seemed to cross his countenance such as I had never witnessed before. But the serenity of his disposition immediately asserted itself. Hercules had crushed Lucifer.

If something haunte-cIMK:I7.-:, it was his secret. Why should I disturb it? If I attempted to raise the curtain, scandal, like a reptile, might hiss at the light and bite my friend. "Sharper than a scorpion's sting is a pard's ' treachery." thought 1, frankly adding aloud: "Mark, I beg yet pardon. Yet interest in Harry Puke is naething to me." He pointed his forefinger at me, and said, in a bantering tone: "You have a woman's curiosity." I stood mumbling sonic frivolous objection, and with a light laugh the happy fellow joined the Senorita, whose chilling smile seemed to humble me in the dust. - -

_ A strange presentiment of evil made me feel as though wire-worms were creeping through my veins. Lucia's lustrous eyes were fixed upon Mark's face. Her remarkable beauty fascinated him, and as they strolled along the shore he placed his arm around her waist, no donbt making love to her. She evidently appreciated it, for a merry ripple of laughter gently echoed among the sandhills. "Pshaw ; she's mocking my ill-humour! " At that moment Pecos pinched my elbow, and nodded significantly at Lucia, his face a study of mingled wonder and perplexity. "The Senorita is a rattlesnake, to be admired at a distance," he observed, "beautiful till she stings. Is Muro, her lover, banished ? " I seized Pecos by the plaited lock of his raven hair, shewed my teeth, knit my brow, and would have cuffed him, but he bobbed; and having broken loose, skidded away to a safe distance, and returned the compliment with a string of words in his vernacular, jerky, grating to the ear, and intensely suggestive of Indian Billingsgate. I gave him the weed of peace and a pinch of snuff. He then aped an ancient British tar, chewed the quid, and danced a kind of hornpipe, screaming "Chee-up!" like a nimble Phillillooeet on a pine bough, and was only reduced to his normal condition after a fit of sneezing. At that moment I turned and saw the superb figure of the Senorita disappearing within the Presidio grounds, and a last glimpse of Mark bending over the Spaniard recalled unpleasant memories. I stood, frowning and baffled. "Strange," I observed half-aloud, "that a wuman, whose wiles an' fascinations are so trans- parent to me, should so singularly attract a robust an brave man like Mark Pepys. She's na a bit wumany, while he combines the boldness o' a lion wi' the simpleecity o' a lad. Her every movement is a graceful pose to win his admeeration. Ah, the world cares leetle fer upright character whaur the deesposition is happy. Bah! I ken Lucia's hypocrisy. She parades her charms, sings her best, dances, panders to his hobbies, an' passes pretty compleements when others fail to appreciate That s the warst o' thae beauties. Why, she glints her een to win his love, shutting not fer aye ony suitable companion wha may chance to cross his path. Aye, Mark, Mark, this blind worship o' the Senorita means meeschief." Such were my communings—not pleasant, but, as I swear, honest enough. With my hands thrust deep in my pockets, my eyes tracing the trail, I wended my way in gloomy silence towards Puke's Delight. On reaching the rough saloon I discovered Harry Puke indulging in forty winks behind his bar, for the festivities at the Presidio" had robbed him of all his customers. The landlord's bald head rested against an oak frame in which a card was inserted bearing the written words of welcome, Bien vienes. Several flies took the hint and alighted on Puke's shiny head, tickling him into restlessness.

Mark's treasures were packed in rough wooden cases, secured with iron bands, and locked in a spare room to the rear of our bedrooms. Precau- tion led me to examine the room, and I satisfied myself that the cases were intact. Now later on I chatted with the genial Puke, and somewhat adroitly led the conversation round to Mark Pepys. "Hae ye noticed the tall Castilian wi' the fine moustache an' rich aristocradc dress—the gitano wha apes the laird ? " "Dunn° his game, Sandy, but he covorts about in that spankin' schooner. Money no end, an' free wi' it." He slapped his pocket significantly. 'A favourite wi' Lucia Diaz, I'm telt." "Is thet so? Darned glad ez somebody knows More about 'n than me. He swaggers a bit, an' even some of our English gals like thet better than common sense. Women are generally mad after foreign goods, worse luck." "Verra true. Stamp an inferior article wi' a foreign trade-mark an the stupid Anglo-Saxon buys at a price. It reminds me o' a husband Oot t' tea, wha praises the host's cookery to the disparagement o' his oon wife's. By the way, it's whispered amang the lads that this man, kuro, soon falls foul 0; onybody wha thwarts his smallest whim. "

"Then some agent in advance is paid to fly his kite, fer ef there's suthin' in it I should hey heard it afore now " ; and he added, shaking his head and slapping his knees to emphasise his opinion: "Ef Puke's Delight ain't in the know, it s some Indian yarn." Then a silence fell between us,. rendered less awkward by our came of draughts. Presently I

A LONG SLTTING,

A meeting of this Council was held in the Co uncil Chambcr at the Town Hall. Wariiuroa, on Tuesday evening. The proceedings lasted over two hours. Tne Mayor (Alderman Wright) presided, and there vrers also present :—Alderenen Fairclough, Harrison, Sutton, Hutchinson, Roberts ; Councillors Shaw Green, Heaton, ('.annel!, Plumpton, Smethurst, Longton, Bennett, John Evans, Ellison, Duncan. James Evans. Furness, Tianion, Peacocke, Glace, J.Alev, Ro4ers, W)ods, F It Roberts, Shillcock, Wilkinson, F. Monks, Crosfield, Lee, Burton, witn Mr. J. Lyon Whittle (town clerk), iktr. Stanley Wilson (deputy town clerk). Mr. S. Fairhurst (borough trcasurer), Mr. T. Longdin (borough surveyor), Mr. Sutcliffe (a,sistant surveyor), Mr. Dew; (sanitary and water engiaem), and Mr. Haddock (gas ellineer). THE NEW POLICE PREAISES—ORIPICISA OF THE

PROPOSED OUT-STATIONS. The MAYOR proposed the adoption of the m inutes.— Al derm an HARRISON seconded. Councillor SKETIEUrtiT, referring to the instruction to the Town Clerk to *poly to the Local Government Boerd for a loan of £5,000 for the erection of cut police stations, said he personally thought the awn a most out- rageous one. No doubt the committee hid carefully considered the matter.but for a town like Warrington to build two out police stations to cot £5,000 when plans Were being submitted for the erection of a main police building estimated to cost something like £15,000 or £16,000 (Councillor Plumptoa £20,000) was not the thing. Be hoped and trusted the Council would show their disapproval of the rensommendetion. He proposed an amendment to the effect that this matter of the out buildings be deferred until the new main police buildings ha I been erected. He Alnuld not object to the spending of money in widening their main thoroughfares, but to ' continue biting at this cherry and biting at thAt was alas surd. He moved that the minute; be passed with the exceptioa of the minute referring to the out police stations. Councillor LONOTON, in seconding the amenernent,said he would like to bear some explanation as to why it was necessary to spend so much money, and why it was necessary to nave the out police statione. He was not anemeeesmsitt)y or end member rfof the ecoimn h me Ittteee' and did not understand the money at all, particularly in view of the coatemelated very large expenditure on the new police station to which they were committed, and which was a great necessity. Councillor BENNETT asked for information with regard to the central stations. They had examinel the plans with a good deal of pleasure and iateresle but tee ex- amination had been superficial and cursory, tie die not know whether the committee had special information beforeoa h ceerint on the streneth of which they decided u in design. The Council should know some' thingthine about tne reasons which had induced the corn- mittee to give preference ti ole over the others. Be, himse'f, considered several of the ethers quite as good. He was pleased to see that two local architects had corn' peted and their designs seemed very good indeed, and he wished they had been thought sufficieatly good to take firSt place: (Hear. hear.) Alderman ROBERTS observed that to a certain extent he felt inclined to support the amendment of Councillor Smethurat, because until the main schema was complete it would be just as well to deter the matter of the out- stations. As long as they had resident police officers, they did not require elaborate police buildings. The out- stittricts were connected with the town police stati a by t aephene, and the very presence of a policeman resi- dent there was a etrong detriment to crime and outrage of any kind. He thought it would be advisable t 3 allow the matter to stand over, though he was leth to apeear in opposition to the recommendation of any committee. With regard to the plans of the main buildings he took it that they were in the hands of the assessor so far as the decision as to the meets of the plans was concerned. It: was quite epee to the Corporation to appoint any other architect, but it would be a poor compliment to Mr. Bennett after they bad committed the matter to him and would show a want of confidence in his judgment if they declined to accept his decision. Both on the grounds of policy and honoer they were bound to accept his decisien. Councillor BENNETT sai lhe was simply a ling for in- formation. Alderman HARRISON said he had hurriedly seconded the adoption of the minutes, and he had for the moment forgotten the matter referred to by Councillor Smethurst. and he hoped the committee would see its way to do what had been suggested. Alderman SUTTON remarked that £5,000 appeared to him to be a very large sum. He thought the expendi- ture would be £2,000. Councillor Trxerion said he was in eetire sympathy with the mover of the amendment. He objected to this extensive expenditure, and argued that at the rate they were going on the new police buildings would cost nearer £30,000 than £16,000. fie was surprised teat such an important minute as that relating to the main station should hay been brought forward without explanation. lie should like the matter to be r sfeired hack until thav could have some figures furnished which would show exactly what position they were going to be in if they p awed these plans. Councillor MONKS Biked why the cost of the proposed out-stations was so much greater than they were led to suppose. The MAYOR said the sites were bought freehold. He also explained that Sir Herbert Croft had insisted for years on two permanent out-stations. Councilor Heterox : It is intended that there should he three—Sanlree Bridges. Winwick read, and Latch- ford. The MAYOR: We are only dealing with two new. The amendment, that the minute relating to the out- stations be not confirmed, WAS then Put and carried. Only Councillors Grace and Jolley voted against it. Councillor CEnSFIELD said he was present. at the meet- ing of the Watch Committee, and heard Mr. Bennett's admirable report, which dealt with eve, y &WI of the internal arrangements of the new police buildings. He nraised the successful plans most highly. He (Ceuneillor Crosfield) did not know,he WAS glad to say,much about the inside of police stations—(laughter)—but it sPemed to h'm that if they could get such a building for £16,000 i would b 3 an ornament to the town and a very cheap building. Councillor MONKS asked if the plans were approved, would the erection of the buildings be _gone on with at once or would the matter be hung up for an indefinite period. The MAYOR said they would be obliged to go on with the matter if the plan were approved. Ceunciller MONKS thought it was customary for the succesaful architect to name a builder who was prepared to carry out the work mentioned. Was there such a guarantee in this case P He also asked if the new build- ing would interfere with the site of the building where the Technical Inetruction Classes are now held. The MAYOR said he thought there would be no difE- cults, in arranging a section of the new premises so as not to interfere with the Technical Institute. Councillor CROSFIELD aid not think it was customary , for an architect to give such a guarantee. , Councillor FURNESS said there should he some definite, understanding with regard to the cost. He moved an amendment that the minute be referred bank to tha Watch Committee, who should fernish at a later date the probable cost of the scheme. Coancillor Megaton seeonded. He objected to Sanc- ti ,ninz the speneine of such a large sum of money. The Tower Cream said that tenders would be adver- tised for, and they could be either accepted or rejected by the °maned!. Alderman ROBERTS remarked that the Watch Corn- mit'ee had acted well in the matter so far. The sweets- fel architect had prepared peens for five or six neliee etatienteand his estimate was likely to be an excesdlnelv r liable sine. If police beildinet were not erected it was certain their grant would be withdrawn. He aided tee, that somehow or other, in spite of the large expendl- ter, each Year, the rate; did not g 0 on. That was a serene indication of the prosperity of the town. (Hear, hear.) Alderman SUTTON said they were obliged to suppler new police amide, and thev most submit to the inevit able, although it was net the best sit 1. Still the Pitn had been selected by the Council, and he would fall in with it. The MAYOR : I objected as strongly as anyone, lout the assessor thinks it a most admirable one. Alderman Roma remarked that the tender.; would have to come before the Council for confirmation. Alderman HARRISON supported the pi.op,eition, and contended that the work should be proceeded with with- out delay.. They had trifled with the matter for eich a long time that it was a wonder the Government officials hand been an patient. Councillor Furrxxss said he was pin IWI with the Woo as shown on paper, hit he thonght before adopting it they should have some estimate of the cost of the pro- posed buildings. Councillor CROSFIRLD : You have got it. The MAYOR £16,5000 Councillor Funismss : It is not an estimste. The MAYOR: It is not a definite estimate. Alderman Fitercuressoer honed no amendment would be submitted,becatre the question had been under the con- sideration of the Council for many years. They could de- 'ar no longer. They would soon he in a fi/I if thee did not commence to build, and the Government grant to- wards the payment of the police would be stopped. The cost was £16,5000, and the assessor must he s near the mark. ; 'mummer uEATON observed that the sleeessful archi- tect had carried out eight or ten other Mans of a similar character, and all had been according to the estimate.

The amendment was lost, only Councillors Tinnion and Furness voting for it, and the minutes of th 3 nem- mittee were approved except those relating to toe pro- posed new ow police stations. Councillor SHAW GREEN alluded to the promotion of Detective Monaghan and Inspector Philips, and with reprd to the latter asked it it was intended he should have an increase in his salary as none was mentioned in , the Chief Constable's report. The MAYOR : I have an impression that he will. , Alderman HUTCHINSON : I don's think it was mei- tioned, but we act according t the scale. div.head: SHIP CANAL COMPANY AND THE DREDGING
div.p: THE SHIP CANAL COMPANY AND THE DREDGING
OF THE MERSEY.

Alderman ROBERTS moved the confirmation of the minutes of the Rivers Committee which stated that the Borough Surveyor submitted a report upon the condi Von of the channel in the Mersey which the Manchester Slip Canal Company are required to keep dredged.—lt was resolved by the committee that notice be served upon the IVlanchester Ship Canal Company requiring them forthwith to dredge the channel in the river as r•quir by the agreemPt of 1896,and that the Town Clerk be in- structed to take all necessary proceedings to enfarc compliance with the agreement. In moving the adop- tion of the recommendations Alderman Roberts Said it. was a long time since the minatos of the committee were of such a serious and important character. The mem- bers of the Council would no doubt have read the very suggestive and important rport which the Borough Surveyor had prepared on the con- dition of the dredging of the river. In order that it might be put in a concise form he would like to state briefly what ths condition of the river was. The total length of the river which the Manchester Ship Canal Company were required to keep dredged to minimum width of 50 feet and a minimum depth of 8 feet was 8,196 lineal yards. The length of this river at present dredged to the required depth and width was only 2,730 lineal yards or considerably less than one-half. The length that had been dredged to the required depth and not to the required width was 1,780 lineal yards. A 9 depth was more important than width the Council would see what a serious condition the river had got into Out of the 6,196 lineal yards which the S'aip Canal Cnm- rany were required to dredge, 3,466 were not in accord- ance with the requirements of the Ship Canal Act. They did not wish to harms or hamper the work of the Ship Canal Company, but when the fact had been proved beyond dispute that the construction of the Shio Canal had permanently damaged the river as a waterway be- tween Liverpool and Warrington, and in anticipation of that possible damag,e an undertaking was given and afterwards incorporated in an Act of Parliament that the Company would dredge that portion of the river within the borough of Warrington. it was absolutely vital to the commercial interests of the town that the Corpora- tion should insist upon the fullest possible carrying out of !the undertaking entered into. (Hear, hear). They „ had had a good deal of correspondence on the subject,

On Friday at the Borough Po ice Court the ad- journed general annual licensing meeting was held for the Borough of Warrington.The Mayor(Alderman Wright) presided on the Bench and there were also with him Aldermen Roberts and Satton,Councillors Pierpoint and Smethurst, Lieutenant Colonel Ridg- way, Messrs. John White, F. W. Monks, T. Birchall, J. W. Hayward, E. J. Guest, and J. Geddes. In the well of the Court there was a fairly-large attend- ance of the general public, including the Rev. E. T. Reed, Mr. A. E. Windle (secretary to the Young Men's Christian Association), Mr. William Roberts, Alderman Bolton and others. The solicitors present were :—Mr. Seger, barrister (instructed by Mr. Longland) on behalf of Mr. William Bolton; Mr. Arthur Browne, on behalf of several applicanta; Mr. W. H. J. Jenkins, on behalf of Mr. James Payton, of the "Blue Back" beerhouse, and Mr. F. R. Roberts, M.A., on behalf of the Temperance Federation. " TEIE PLEASURE BOAT ROUSE" AND

" HAWTHORN " LICENSES. Mr. Arthur Browne said he was instructed to apply on behalf of Joseph H. Clarke, for the final grant confirm- ing the provisional licence of what was formerly known as the "Pleasure Boat House " but what was proposed to be named the Causeway Hotel. The building had been completed, and the Chief Constable had been through it. He would simply call Mr. Owen who would prove that with the exception of a slight deviation from the plans formerly submitted, the plans had been carried out as deposited. The alteration which had 10.. en made was, he wai given to understand, an improvement to the house. . . .

Mr. Owen, architect, was then called, and explained the slight alteration which had been made. The Chief C3astable said the alteralon was a distinct improvement. It had made two rooms int) one large room. Mr. Browne said the requisite notices had been served. The bench granted the app!icatioa. Mr. Browne then made a similar application with reference to the Hawthorn lan, Orford-lane, of which Joseph Backard is tenant. A slight deviation had also been made from the plans in this case. The Chief Constable was consuted, and Mr. Owen would be able to tell the Bench that the alt3ration of two rooms into one was far better than if the plans had been carried out in their eatirety end two separate rooms made. The Chief Constable : I can quite en lorse what Mr. Browne has said. Mr. Owen thou explained the alteration which bad been made. The Mayor (to Uri Chief Constable) : Are you satis- fied with the tenant ? The Chief Constable : Quite satisfied. I should like to know when the Little Horse Shoe will be closed ? Mr. Browne: At once._ _ . _

The Chief Constable said the agreement was that for this fully-licensed house the owners were to give up the Little Horse Shoe and the Shannon and Chesapeake, and for the Blacksmith's Arms, the Bull's Head, and the Harp and Crown. The Little Horse Shoe had not yet been closed although the Bull's Head had been for some time. Mr. Browne said with regard to the Little Horse Shoe, there had been some slight mistake. They had been under the impression that the Little Horse Shoe was to be given u 9 for the Bla.cksrmith's Arms. But arrange- ments were being made to close the Little Hone Shoe on the 10th October. . . .

The Chief Constable said that if that was satisfactory to the Bench he would hot make any objection. Alderman Sutton : It doesn't make much difference. This application was then granted. "TEE OLD HOUSE AT HOYIE."—APPLICkTION FOR A WINE LICENSE. _

Mr. Arthur Browne then appiied for a wine license on behalf of Thomas Mullins for the "Old House at Borne" beeroouse, Friars' Green. Be daresay the magistrates would think they were applying for a wine license to supply the immediate neighbourhood. But that was not So. Tho house was a good one, and Mr. Mullins did not get one-fifth of his custom from Friars'-green. R3B. p sctable friends came to see him from time to time, who required asiae. Me house WAS also used by travel- lers and theatricals. 'Dais was not an attempt to increase the drinking facilities of the neighbourhood. A supper was held at the house the other evening in connection with the. National Amalgamated Society of Operative House and Ship Painte:s and Decorators and they asked for wine but could not get it. Mr. Mullins wag called upon to give evidence in sup port of the application,but he had not put in an appear- ance, and other applications were heard. Later on he went into the witness-box, and said a wine license was badly needed. He was repeatedly asked for wine. Mr. A. E. Windle (Secretary of the Younz Men's Christian Association) gui he had been requested by the Committ,e of the Young Men's Christian Association to oppose any further grant to the house in question. Mr. Monks : There is not the same public n6cessity in this case as in the case of the Blue Back.
. - Mr. Brown: A small &ass of port would do a man less harm thin a glass of beer. Alderman Sutton: I think that is an impartant factor in the case.
Mr. Browne : We do not apply for the neighbourhood. Alderman Roborts : non what does the house exist at all for ? .

Mr. Browne : lam applying to the committee. Alduman Roberts : But lam one of the confirming magistra'es, and if Alderman Sutton is allowed to speak I shall take the same opportunity. If the house does not exist for the want of the ne4hboarhoad what does it exist for? Mr. Browne : That is my case,and the Chief Constable has no objection. The Chief Constab'e : I have no objection except on the one point raised that it is not necessary for the needs of the neighboarhood.

ALDERMAN BOLTON'S NEW LICENSE CONFIRMED. Mr. Segar applied on behalf of William Bolton for a confirmation of a grant of an alehouse license for a locus to be constructed at the junction of Parr-street and Percival-street. Ha said this matter was thrashed out at the annual licensing meeting, and he should therefore, say very little before Introducing evidence. Of course the questions which would arise, and which would have to be considered on the application, were the character ,of the applicant, the character if the house, Its suita- bility for the purpose for which it was proposed to be built, and the wants of the neighbourhood. In those matters Alderman Bolton had a vary strong case. The site of the proposed house was in the centre lof an area in which public house accommodation was very scarce, and it was proposed not only to absorb an eff-grocer's license into the full license —which of course, was not like creating a new facility for drinking purposes—but it was proposed to abolish in a district where public-houses were to be found in great ittumbers an old established public-house called the Crown I That was situated off Bridge-titreet,and class to Market. gate. The Rose, a beerhouse in Dial-street, close to the court, would also be given up. He thought the young gentleman who represented the Young Men's Christian Astrciation could not have been fully instructed, because I they were not asking for an additional license—they were really asking for permission to Er gilder a license from a part of the town where public-houses abounded I to a neighbourhood where they were net in evidence. Mr. Longland here informed Mr.Segar that the Secre- tary of tbe Young Men's Christian Association was not opposing this license, but Mr. Mullins' application. Mr.Segar said it was evident, then, that the Secretary of the association had fully investigated the matter and found that no opposition to his application would be of any avail. Alderman Bolton was well known in Warrington, and had acquired by his energy. tact,and good management an exceptionally good character with regard to the management of a house. Be hid as high a character as any of the great brewers cf the town. The plans of. the new house had been designed with a view to meeting all the require- ments and all the suggestions which had been made from time to time with regard 'lto the building of such houses. The public accommodation would be ample, and the house part would be quite separate from the public part of the house. The nearest house to the north was the Bull's Head, 580 yards away, and to the south the Leeh Arms. The fact that the nearest public-house was 580 yards away, was a very strong fact in proof of the assertion that Alderman Bolton had a very. strong case. The popu- lation was quite 2,000 in a radius of a quarter of a mile As the magistrates would know, the Corporatioa pro- posed to make a !ridge over the Mersey at Howley, and the traffic from Warring`oa Bridge would thus be diverted,makint Parr-street a very important thorough fare. The traffic would be very large, And the proposed houso would be a very great convenience to persons passing that way. Aldarm in Bolton's great experience and interest in those houses were a guarantee that he would continue the high csurse of conduct that he had ruccassfully pqrsued hitherto. It was quite clear that the Secretary of the Christian Association had done wisely in not opposing such an applicat'on which was Po good, aisd which would not intertere with the Young Men's Christian Society.

div.p: THE NEW POLICE BUILDINGS FOR

TILE ACCEPTED DESIGN.

Eighteen competitive designs were sent in to the Corporation from architects in various Parts of the offices, police arolYn o the site of the Ea ni an gedooronan efrnrs tcho eu rnte, wt cb neerteacbtue Old Barracks in Arpley-street Mr. Bennett, presi- dent of the Manchester Society of Architects, was appointed assessor, on the nomination of the Presi- dent of the Royal Institute of British Architects. The plans, with sections, &c., were exhibited in the Council Chamber at the Town Hall, and on Tuesday the assessor presented his report, the first premiated design accepted being that of Mr. R. Burns Dick, architect, 55, Northumberland-street, Newcastle-ou- Tyne, who is, according to the arrangement, entitled to the sum of £100; but the committee have decided to recommend him as the architect, and he will, therefore, superintend the carrying out of his own plans. The selection has given general satisfaction, and there is no doubt the new police premises, sm., will be an ornament to the town, a credit to the architect, and of great con- venience to the . Chief Constable, the men under his charge. solicitors, press, witnesses, and others who will have to make use of them In his report Mr. B. urns Dick states that the most. careful consideration has convinced him that to ob- tain anything like a perfect plan embodying all the i accommodation asked for tis necessary to entirely clear the site and so do away with the old armoury las well as the other buildings existing at the Old barracks After referring to the aecommodatioe his plan provides for cells, public officers, parode iroom and courts, he says the style of the buildlnZe he has adopted had not been upon any particular period of architectural history but was the natural outcome of the plan treated in what, for want of la better nomenclature, might be termed Free Renaissance adapted to suit the materials proposed to be used, A broad simplicity was aimed at not only because of the limited cost but because of it being more suited to the nature of the build- ings. It is, proposed to build them of brick, exter- nally faced to the front with a good deep red pressed brick with buff terracotta dressings. The staircases will be of stone or hard granolithic, with patent non-slipping treads. The internal walls with the exception of the cellblockwailnldbewphlearseteirteids.prlnt- s psisuorpse steam erdoiatoedhoat n voewtwhaeordm the bupling with low pres- sure panels double pipe return system. Mr. Dick further says in his report that he has gone carefully into the cost of the buildings and found that they would cost about £16,500. We may add that he has been engaged on similar buildings for three cities and Borough Corporations. The second premiated design is that of Messrs. Tapper and Crouch, architects.l2,Gray's Inn-square, London, W.C,, who receive £5O. The third design is that, of Mr. J. Lane For, architect, Bond-street, Dewsbury, who receives £25. On Saturday afternoon, Bradley flail Farm. Applotoo, belonging to Mr. John Marsh, who i 3 w,ll-known in Warrington, and throughout the county, was the scene of one of the most extensive farm fires which has occurred for many years in Cheshire. It. is said Mr. Marsh's is the largest stack yard in Cheshire. The fire broke out abent four o'clock, but how it originated is a mystery. There were 25 stacks of coris, wheat and hay stored on the premises, eleven of which were under a large dutch wooden barn with a slate roof, The Lymm Fire Brigade under the direction of Mr. lt,..use were first on the scene. Shortly after the Warrington Brigade i with the steam fire engine Major n charge of E gineer Ratcliffe arrived, being suarnonel by telegram. Mr. ince with the wilderspool Brigade took the Empress engine and tefore long the three brigades 'were playing on the burning stacks. A rod supply of water was oh- taed from an old. moat on the premises. it was s.en that notwithstanding their efforts most of the stacks were doomed. One shed containing eleven wanks was completely destroyed in addition to seven other stacks and a but. Late on Saturday night two brigades left men in charge. They continued producs all the night and tiseo: playnvdinagy ent and in er nmr tonhu? en evening iri were relieved by other Warrington firemen who remained on duty until Tues. and £1,500 and is covered by insurance_ day afternoon at 3 o'clock.
