APPARENTLY the Canadian Prohibition By Plebiscite. pl6biscite on the subject of

the Prohibition of the Liquor Traffic has failed to give a sufficiently definite re- sult to warrant legislation. The returns are not quite complete, but there appears to have been only a small vote polled, and the net result is a meagre majority for prohibition—about 20,000. The poll shows that there is a preponderance oi feeling in the Dominion generally in favour of the legislative suppression of the liquor traffic ; but, as a large body of electors have not taken the trouble to record their votes, it can hardly be claimed that a clear majority of the electorate de- biro prohibition. IVloreover, the prbvince of Quebec and most of the large towns have given majorities against it. In face of this rather dubious result Sir WILFRID LAURIER will hardly consider him- self warranted in proposing a prohibitory law for the whole Dominion. The experience of the pl - biscite, on the other hand, rather establishes a case for provincial Home Rule on the subject, or what is called Local Option. But a Local Option Liquor Act Canada already possesses. Perhaps the question submitted to the popular vote was worded too absolutely. It was: "Are you in favour of the passing of an Act prohibiting the importation, manufacture, or sale of spirits, wine, ale, beer, cider, and all other alcoholic liquors for use as beverages? This, it will be seen, is very extreme; it allows no intermediate degrees of pro- hibition. The Temperance party are to be con- gratulated on having to say the least, obtained a majority on such a definite and clear-cut issue. But the probability is that the sweeping character of the question prevented many electors from answer- ing with a direct " Yes " or" No," and hence the indefinite character of the vote.

IThis is not the first time there have been plebis- cites taken on the question in Canada; but previous cases were only local provincial votes. Generally they showed large majorities for prohibition—in fact, larger local majorities than the same pro- vinces have given now. It is the lazy elector,who ' will not make up his mind to give a definite "Yes' or "No," and halts between two opinions, who has rendered the Dominion pleibiscite practically non-effective. It is to be feared that there will always bo a similar stumbling block to the success of popular plebiscites like this. The present experiment, it has been pointed out,is not an instance of the "Referendum" The "Re- ferendum " refers a measure already before the Legislature to a vote Gf the people. The Canadian plebiscite asked the people whether there was to be legislation on certain lines, leaving the form of the bill to be drawn thereon to Parliament. The re- ference to the people of a bill already before Par- liament would probably result in an even more puzzling and doubtful answer being returned than ' this. Many electors might favour the general ' r principle of the measure, but object to particular clauses. They would therefore refrain from vot- ing for" the bill, the whole bill, and nothing but the bill " ; and if a majority were recorded against it owing to these reservations,the resu't would not boa true verdict. The Canadian form of plebis- cite is not so open to practical objections as the Referendum. Still, :;t may be that the too abso-
lute terms in which the question submitted has been drawn up has deprived the Temperance party of the popular victory they might otherwise have obtained.
TIIE water famines in East The Water Problem. London and several provincial

towns have directed attention afresh to what has become, perhaps, one of the most difficult national problems. The case of Lon- don, doubtless, stands"first order urgent." It is the metropolis, and there the densest mass of human- ity is crowded together within a limited area. The inhabitants of the East and North-east districts of London have suffered great privations during the long spell of dry weather. But from state- ments made at the London County Council on I Tuesday,it would seem that the greater part of the metropolis stands in danger of a failure of one of the elements of life. Not only has the Lea, from which East London gets its water,been practically sucked dry,but the Thames, the other main source of the metropolitan supply, is running alarmingly , low. The companies which take their water from the Thames ought to leave a flow over Teddington Weir of not less than two hundred million gallons per day. But in September the quantity only averaged eighty-six million gallons per day, while in one day it was reduced so low as fifty millions. The Thames stream had now dwindled so low that a few days rain would only stir up the mud, and make the water undrinkable. Undoubtedly the case of the metropolis is becom- ing alarming, though there are districts which still obtain a copious supply from the chalk and other sources. But even the County Council is not so impressed as it ought to ,be with a sense of its responsibility in the matter. At a "full dress debate" on the Water question, on Tuesday, much indignation was expended on the East Lon- don Water Company, but after all, the Council adjourned the discussion without coming to any conclusion on the resolutions submitted to it. The East London Water Company is apparently an incorrigible-offender. Its dereliction of duty lies in the fact that, until the scarcity was actually upon it, it failed to put into operation its statu- tory powers to connect its mains with those of other London companies, so that the sru plus of one district might be available for the needs of another. The work of connecting mains takes weeks to complete, and it is only now that the stress in the most populous part of London is being relieved. Both the company and the Government are to blame for their remissness in this matter. And even the London County Coun- cil seems unable to make up its mind how to meet the emergency. The question is not the superiority of municipal over private supply. Several municipal supplies have failed during the past summer. The question is, where to get more water with the least possible delay. To obtain a new, pure. and adequate supply for London from Wales, or elsewhere, will entail a work of years. The case of Birmingham has been almost as bad as East London, and there the whole responsibility rests on the municipality. Liverpool and Manches- ter, in past years, before they went to Lakes Vytnwy and Thirlmere, often experienced water famines more or less acute. It took years to make those sources available. Birmingham is now tapping the head waters of the Wye in Mid Wales, but the work has already occupied two or three years, and it will take as much longer. Other towns are casting about for watersheds to annex. The whole subject of water supply is one with which Parliament should deal, in the interests of the entire nation.

' We feel quite sorry for the Mandi. He is being mutilated in the most unconscionable manner by people who certainly ought to know better, The latest story from the Nile valley is that Major Gordon, a nephew of the hero of Khartoum, has secured the defunct Moslem's head, which he in- tends to keep as a curio—and perhaps revengefully gloat over it, who knows F A few officers described as being "not over-fastidious," have possessed themselves of the Mandi's toe and finger nails "as mementoes." This dismemberment of a dead foe is rather disgusting. The British Army might be composed of pagans and officered by savages to judge by the reports from the front. We can not.and do not expect a strict observance of all the canons of civilization in the Soudan, but it is surprising to us to find British officers of some celebrity so far forgetful of good taste and decency as to coolly seize "a mementoes "portions of the long-buried anatomy of a foe, however atrocious a character he may have been when alive.

The London County Council has framed a num- ber of new and excellent by-laws, which came into force on Saturday. They will tend to lessen the thousand and one things which go to make life in the metropolis almost destitute of enjoyment or comfort. Street betting, for one thing, will be rendered a pastime of much more considerable difficulty and danger to the participators in L, than hitherto. But it is the annoyances which most beset the citizen when at home against which the new by-laws are principally directed. He need no longer endure in impotent resentment the peace-disturbing howlings of his neighbour's dog, the brayings of his ass, the cackling of:his fowl, or other unpleasant noises caused by the domestic pet next door. He now has his remedy, and has only to find two other citizens who agree with him that the said animal is causing a " serious nuisance," and the owner gets notice that unless the brute learns better manners in a fortnight, proceedings, with pains and penalties follow. Steam round- abouts and kindred devices for amusing the young anti driving the adults to the verge of insanity, similarly come under the ban of the law in London. They must cease their incessant " toot- ings," their mangling of popularairs,their obstruc- tion of traffic, if the citizen finds them a " nuis- ance." Lucky London I How we in provincial towns envy you your sensible by-laws, and what a campaign against " nuisances" we would com- mence if the authorities would only put the power in our hands!

The Anglo-American rapprochment has been the subject, this week, of an interview with Senator F. D. Pavey, now staying in London. This gentle- man's views on such a universally interesting question are rightly deemed important, as he is a , trained pohtican and a rising man in the public life of America. Senator Pavey says the feeling of friendliness towards this country is a national one in America, and by no means confined to any one sect or party. It has been growing for the last twenty years, and now, to use his own words "the ties of race language, and institutions have sur- vived the memories of old conflicts." We in this country feel gratified at the evident approach of a union between the two great English-speaking nations of the earth, and look forward with plea- sure to its consnmmation. But this feeling of joy •8 tempered by disappointment. Animus, accord- ling to Senator Pavey, is still felt against this country by the American-Irish, who appear irreconcilable, and prone to rake up old grievances and probe partially-healed wounds. Yet there is hope that the memory of the sym- pathy of this country with the Americans in ther late conflict with Spain, may be effective in dis- persing the dark thoughts of the unreconciled Irish. They are now part and parcel of the American nation, and if the German element in the states can—as the Senator asserts it can—join heartily with the native Americans in their feeling of cordiality to England, surely our erstwhile neighbours can "bury the hatchet,"and extend the

hand of peace and friendship too, Even should they stand aloof, this friendly feeling is so Pre- dominent in the States,that the two nations ought inevitably to become cemented together in the near future.

After the decision of the Warrington Licensink Committee last August it was perhaps only nature. 1 to expect that a sufficient number of in , trates woud be found at the adjournea licensing meeting last Friday to accept the bai of Mr. William Bolton to "surrender " certain licenses of more or less value for permission be erect a large hotel at the junction of Parr an,. Percival-streets with a full license attached. -1.1 property owners suffer by the deterioration 0 property in this district in consequence of this addition to the facilities f drinking, or if the moral tone of th neighbourhood is appreciably lowered thereby t sufferers must hold the magistrates responsible f it. Considering the comparative ease with which. brewers and licensed persons are able to get ' applications acceded to in Warrington it - rather surprising that one application should be refused on Friday. But this was perhaps te° wild an application even for a Warrington bench of magistrates to accede to. Here was a case of licensee applying for a wine license when almost within a stone's throw there are several hotels more than sufficient to meet the demands of the neighbourhood and of as many wine-drinking tra- ' Yellers as visit the town

The difficulties in the way of a correct adminis- tration of the new vaccination Act seem to be innumerable, and all sorts of interpretations .of the measure have been acted upon by the mag,is- trates. Quite a number of justices, apparentlY believers in vaccination, have taken to arguing with the applicant for exemption, in a manner scarcely seemly and quite illegal. It goes against the grain with these gentlemen when they are asked for a certificate by a man who contents him .- self with expressing in half-a-dozen words his conscientious objection to vaccination. They will persist in arguing, and asking the why and the wherefore of his objection. These things they are not called upon to do. A parent's, or guardian s avowal of conscientious objection is all that the Act entails upon him in applying for an 'exemption certificate. With regard to the granting of these certificates a custom has become general of charging is. 6d. or 2s. as a fee. There is no clause in the Act, we believe, which authorises a magistrate to demand any fee what- ever for the certificate. In a case at Warrington last week—the first ono locally by the way—the applicant was charged is. for his certificate, ar- ceeding which we venture to think was withom Justification by law. Otherwise the bench took very commonsense view of the case, and their per- formance of the new duty laid upon them was marked by impartiality. It is clear that some authoritative ruling will have to be given ere benches of magistrates up and down the country can be expected to show conformity with the strict letter of the law on vaccination, and uni- formity of action with each other.

-- The new Anglo-German agreement, as interpre- ted by the Fortnightly Review, looks authentic, and it has the merit of being fair. Portugal is undoubtedly preparing for a slow withdrawal frora her costly possessions in Africa. We cannot desire to have them all, but on the other hand ive might prevent Germany from getting them, and it is to Germany's interest to come to an arrange' ment with us before Portugal throws the whole of her colonies on the market. It has been more than once baid thas it would be a stupid and inexcusable blunder on the part of Lord SalisburY to negotiate with Germany concerning our rights to Delagoa Bay. In international law our clairos to that region are above suspicion, but then the Concert of Europe does not always bow to the law, and Germany could have stirred up serious trouble for us even though she might not ultimately have been able to prevent our occupation. The gist of the agreement seems to be that skeguarantees not to conspire against our acquisition of Delagoa Bay, and on our part Lord Salisbury promises to facili- tate the acquisition by Germany of a fair share of the Portuguese possessions in Africa. These pos- sessions have a very considerable latent value, which the Portuguese are too indolent, too poor, and too terrified of malaria to develope. It is for the common benefit that they should pass into ti possession of more vigorous owners, and so long our just rights are respected no one will complain that Germany has been admitted as co-heir with Great Britain. Mr. Charles Williams's revelations as to thel treatment accorded to the war correspondents in • the lecent campaign will not strike the public favourably. It must be borne in mind that the Sirdar did not want any war correspondents,except one, a civilian friend whO represented an agency'. Public opinion, acting through the Foreign Office, compelled the Sirdar to make provision for all correspondents of duly accredited newspapers. Lord Kitchener issued the permits, but then, according to Mr. Williams, showed his resentment by all kinds of slights and hardships, many of these striking at the health of the men. They were compelled to herd with nogroes, some of their' described as leprous ; they were left to sleep in the drenching rain without tents or beds, they were several times ordered to be at certain places at fixed hours, and were then kept waiting, perhaPe , for seven hours,in the burning sun without shelter or food. The transport, for which they paid high prices, was shamefully bad. All these things maY be said to be incidentals ia the harsh game of war, but it is singular that officers and soldiers should not have been exposed to them. It may be looked upon as ungrateful to criticise a distinguished soldier who has just rendered valuable se-vices to his country. At the same time,it must be pointed out that war correspondents are sent to the front at the express desire of the public, and when the civilian public and the military come into conflict in these matters, it is not right that inn oceut intermediaries should be the scapegoats. War. correspondents, time and again, have willingly spilt' their blood and lost their lives in the public ser: vice. All they ask in return is considerate and
courteous treatment, and opportunity to do their work without vexatious interference.

4.,441 *,.[BY A CORRESPONDENEI FOOTEIALL. Leighs's visit to Runcorn was all that it was ex- pected to be, and came up to the general expecta- tion—a close and hard game—minus anything ex- ceptionally brilliant; save of course the gratifying victory for the boys in green.

Of the visitors perhaps the honours f3r smartness of tackling and tactics are due to Molyneux and Coleman, but Dunbavin also was there, and useful too, though a trifle funky. Still the crow I need not have said "that he was afraid of " little Charlie Butterworth"—it's unkind. Perhaps he didn't want to hurt him? What does Charlie say? Warder was good, and at times displayed some fine qualities, but Wilkinson was also en evidence and is a consistent player. The "Old 'en" and 4. Young 'un"—Houghton and C Butterworth— played a capital game, the former in his usual safe manner, and the latter with promising dash. Walker as a three-quarter, could not be called a success, but he cams up to expectations and no one was dissatisfied. The forwards worked bard,but as a body were often bested by the opposing pack.

On the whole, the game was a very even one, and neither side cold boast of having anything in hand. At times it was poor to look upon—nothing but kick and scramble-74f others it would brighten up, but not for long ;if it got going fairly it was brought up by the referee's "toot," for some minor infringe- ment.

Glancing at the team selected to face Widnes on Saturday at Widnes, one is pleased to see the name of George Robinson at half. But the reason for the change of 0 wen Ilughss into the thrae-quarters, and S. Walker back again into the forwards is not quite app„ent• Somehow or other I don't care for this ex oerimenting especially for class-matches.

I see that the Runcorn Committee have refused to grant the transfer of J. Butterworth and J. Faulkner to Warrington, notwithstanding the fact that the Warrington Committee made the Runcorn Club an exceedingly goof offer. This is rather hard on the two players,a interests my opinion, not the best way of serving the of the Runcorn F.C. Butterworth and Faulkner have refused to tarn out for Runcorn, so what possible good can there be in refusing their transfer to Warrington ? None,l say. y The Rancorn Club gain nothing, and lose a round sum of atoneY. which would go a long wa towards putting them in a sound financial position. Why should they not give these players the transfer they themselves desire ? The relations between the two clubs are of the most friendly ?iature, and I hope that the Runcorn Committee will reconsider their decision and make the i best bargain possible. At present the only bargain made s a bad bargain for the Club, and enforces idleness on the two players concerned.

"Hope Hall," Bridge-street, has at one period of its existence been the sheltering roof of "The Gos- pel Mission"—that is if one draws conclusions from a legend to that effect depicted upon the lamp which overhangs the entrance. Now* however it Ins de- generaten. And oftentimes the proprietor of some "penny-gaff" can be heard extolling, the merits and wonders which he will exhibit for a penny,from the steps thereof. There is nothing to lament about in this ; but one would think that the situation would be less incongruous if the inviting " Clasp sl Mission Room "were removed from the lamp.

Mr. Walter Collier again brings before the Urban Council the question of the baths; and this tim3 he does so with a threat. He says : "the matter shall not rest till I see it through." Ones before he used a threat and I feal justifiKl in reminding my readers that at a previous meeting (July 7th) Mr. Collier said " that he for one would not let the matter rest." Ziat was in the matter of the electric light; and from th 3 sparks that ware flying about at yesterday's meeting, it is evident that Mr. Collier moans to keep the "pot boiling."

Mr. Wilson's remark that it was a social, sanitary, awl moral obligation on the part of the Council to provide baths, touches the crux of the whole affair; and it would be well to keep that point in view, for it is certainly nothing more nor less than a social obligation that mikes anyone indulge in a wash. It is not an amusement, and no one does it for the fun of the thing. Yet, even though it is ob- ligatory, it is none the less a necessity, and being so should he provided for. -- Mr. Gatley's accusation to f inconsistency is un- warranted—for on the authority of Sir Wemyss Reid, the editor of Mr. Gladstone's biography, " Apparent inconsistency is the highest proof of consistency." Thus, though the conduct of the several members appears antagonistic to anything in the shape of a baths scheme, one can easily see at a second glance, that they are actuated by motives for proceeding cautiously, and in their opinion for the best.

div.head: RUNCORN DISTRICT NURSE FUND.
div.p: RUNCORN DISTRICT NURSE FUND.
ANNUAL MEETING.

At the Council Chamber, Town Hall, Runcorn, on Monday afternoon, the annual meeting of the Runcorn District Nurse Fund t3ok place, presided over by the Ray. Canon M.itland Wood (vicar of the parish). There were also pressnt—Mr. S. Taylor (hon. treasurer), Mr. J. W. Lightburn,and the f allowing ladies : Mrs. Imison. Mrs. Wnittaker, Mrs. Barker, Mrs. W. Timmins, Mrs. F. Norman and Mrs. Kay. . _ . . .

The report subnlitted showAd that n'ne years had posed since the first district nurse went out to attend the sick of the town of Runcorn, and every succeeding year from the first had shown convincinely the many advantag,e3 the people derived from the fund. The committee wished to express their sense of the value 07. the small fund for the sending of invalid children, and it was not out of peace to add that a fund for convalescent adults would he of the greatest possible service. The total number of visits paid by the nnrse was as follows : Cases 2,018, oceasional visits 981, total 3,027. As com- pared with last year there was an increase of 509 visits. The number of cases which had been visited was 88, viz. : Medical, 45 cases, 785 visits ; surgical 33, 1,010 visits ; typhoid 9, 202 visits ; chronic 1, 49 visits; total 88 cases, 2,046 visits. Of these 51 were convaleseent,l7 had died, and 20 remained on the book • 13 had been sent to convalescent homes. 96 patients had been visited occasionally and received 981 visits. Tot 1,1 number of persons visited during the year,lB4. The members of the committee to retire this year were Mrs. Abel, Mrs. McLennon,and Mrs. Maitland Weod. Owing to the re- moval from the town of Mrs. Preston there was a fourth vacancy to be filled. —Tte report was adopted. Mr.S.Taylor,(hon.treasurer),reported that the receipts during the year were £l2B 5s 7d., and the expenditure reached only £94 11 21; leaving a b l'ance in hand of £34 43 58. .

As a testimony of the appreciation in the town of the work of the fund, the ctiairman read a letter from a workingman's wife to a nurse, thanking her for her kindness and attention shown. The thres retiring members of the committee—Mrs. Able, Mrs. McLennan, and Mrs. Wood—were re-elected on the proposition of Mrs. Bay, seconded by Mr. Taylor. Mrs. Barker moved, and Mrs.VValter Timmins Mandel, and it was resolved that Mrs. H 41.111 e be electei to fill the vacancy caused by Mrs. Preston's removal. Upon the motion of the Chairman, seconded by Mrs. Whittaker, Mr. S. Taylor was re-elected treasurer. Votes of thanks conclacled the meeting.

PARISH COUNCIL MEETINGS.—On Tuesday evening, the , Frodsham Parish Council, acting as a Par ochial Corn- mittee, met at the Patty Sessional Court loue, Main- street, convened specially for the purpose of considering the question of adopting the proposed scheme for the j supplying of water to Frod3tram Lordship. There were I present i—Messrs. Caarles Linakor (in the chair), j Thomas Earlam, J. W. Rothwell. James Hillidge, F. W. , Spencer, John Barrow, W. E. Shore, J. J. Wilkin- son, T. Hulse, J. G. The scheme be- ing est'mated to cost £3,000 or thereabouts.—& deputa- tion of the Frodsham Lordship Committee was received, and the matter was generally discussed.—Upon the re- tirement of the deputation, it was decided, by 8 votes to 3 votes, that the scheme be adopted.—Subsequently there was a meeting of the Frodsham Lordship Com- mittee, and on the motion of Mr. Thomas, seconded by Mr. Lewis, it was resolved, that the Clerk make applica- tion to the Local Government Board for sanction to borrow the money to carry out the proposed works.

SOLVING THE BATHS QUESTION.
Mr. W C Tier moved " that the Urban District Coun- cil of Runcorn do hereby adopt, the lo%ths and Wash- houses Acts of 1816, 1847, 1873 and 1882,"

, Mr. unison seconded. Mr. Grice questioned whether it would land the Coun- cil into any expense ;or would i at any time compel them into a forilei expenditure. Mr. Lake (the law clerk) : The a loption costs noth- ing, and any further acti in taken under it will be re- viewed by the Counifil. Mr. Bisbrown said he thought they could net raise any objection to the passing of the resolution ; as anything further, would have to come before the Council. They were not binding themselves to anything. If Mc. Collier would not take it amiss of him to say so he hoped he would not land them into unnecessary expense. Mr. Collier It is only like " [Lssinl the cruet," it costs nothing. (Laughter). Mr. W. Handley c ensidered that the proposer ef such a motion shoisld be prepared to give some informati )n as to the extent and operation e the Act, it was only fair that the position of the Council should be defiaed. Be was ignorant on the point, and he believed that most of the members round that table were in a similar posi- tion to himself. (Hear, heir.) There was not one in the room who did not feel the need of baths and who did not slmpethise with that need. The baths question bad been discussed by them for a long time past, and now it wasifound necessary to take that step. He was even prepared to pay his share in the expense of a public bath ; but still they ought to know something more than a mere resolution. If that information was not forthcoming, it would be far better even to adjourn the question to a future date, and consider it in committee meanwhile. - - - -

Mr. Lightb Ira : Perhaps Mr. Collier is prepared to give us some information ? The Chairman also said that hi should lik3 to know the position of the Council;and whether, if soma persons took it into their heads to do so, could the Council be forced into a compulsory provision of baths and wash. houses. He thought perhaps a dozen people or so might have that power. The Law Clerk said that he was not prepares to give a vpty,and that Act was so voluminous. Under the old Act a two-third majority in vestry was required, but he could not say what was requisite now. Mr. Collier : I should like to hear a further expres- sion from the other members. Mr. VVilsen consldered that it devolved itself into a question of" how do we stand with the public ; what is the Council's position in regard to them ?" He did not like shelving an important (location. The ;Law Clerk : You represent the public your- selves. Mr. Wilson further said that he looked upon the pro- vision of baths as a sanitary and moral obligation,and the resolution of Mr. C sllier had his support,considering the information he had for the moment. Mr. Imisen e pnosed that almost every Parish Council in the district had adopted the Act. It was their duty, he thought, to press this matter forward so that the thing could be taken on is merits when the time Came. .

Mr. Taylor said he r eferred in his remarks more par- ticularly to Washhouses. Mr. Gatley said he wan not surprised that Mr. Collier wanted more infomation from the members. The baths question had been a plank in a great many of the elec- tion platforms of those who bad got on the Council. Some said they were ready to pay their share of the costs even. He was glad of that,and hoped it would go forth, but when it came to a question of their vote they went against the scheme. They were inconisten4. Whilst pretending to sympathise with the scheme they voted agains it. He gusted some lamentable instances of boys being drowned through ignorance of the natatory art. Mr. Grice sail that he was not averse to baths if the ratepayers supported them, but it was a question of ex- pense. Were the ratepayers prepared t 3 face a deficiency and expense on their working ? Mr. Wilson said that he had had a lot to do with 'gentlemen concerned in municipal government, and in all cases they told him that- the working of puhlic baths was always at a loss. They, in Runcorn, paid for the 1 removal of the nightsoil; not as a matter of business, ot remuneration but as a social necessity. Mr. Lighthurn said in answer to Mr. Wilsen, with 1 regard to the night soil, they were compelled to attend to that, whilst the question of baths was a matter they could as vet please themselves about. 1 Mr. Collier said his reason for the moving of that resolution was because he was desirous of proceeding in regular form. If he had neglected that step and brought forward another baths soheme, they would be the first to tell him he was out of order, and would have to set about getting that Act adopted. They must not think that the public were not cognisant of what was taking place. For they werc ; and it was high time to take a step in that direction. When the Act was adop- ted, they might depend upon it,they would always have a scheme before them, for he would never allow the thing to drop until be had seen it through. The motion having been put to the vote The Chairman remarked "Uraanicnously Mr. Collier." Mr. C ellier : Thank you ; and it has CDit nothing. (Laughter.) The proceedings then terminated.

div.head: WARRINGTON CORPOIMION AND THE FEATHERS' HOTEL LICENSE.
div.p: THE WARRINGTON CORPOIMION AND THE FEATHERS' HOTEL LICENSE.

DISCUSSION AT THE TOWN COUNCIL MEETING. At the meeting of the Warrington Town Council on Tuesday evening an animsted diseussion took place with reference to the recommendation of the General Purposes Committee :—" That the license of the Feathers Hotel, Bridge-street, be given to Mesirs, Peter Walker and San, Limited, in exchange for the proposed improvement of Queen-street, and the strip of land in front of the Lion Hotel, in Bridge-street." Councillor SHAW-GREEN said he should like the com- mittee t give the Council a plal,if there was one, show- i rig the proposed improvement in Queen-street. The TowN Cmix : It is on the table.

Alderman ROB&RTS said he had beti hoping that the Mayor was going to propose the confirmation of the minutes of the committee with the exception of the one relating to the Feathers Hotel, but as he had not done so he (Alderman Roberts) would move an amendment to that effect. He moved that the resolution of the com- mittee be not confirmed, and he would tell the Council why he did so as briefly as he could. At the last meet- ing of the Council he indicated the lines upon which he should go en a future occasion, and a further consideia- bon of the subject in the meantime had confirmed him in the views lee then expressed. He thoiight that it would be better in the interests of the town if the license in question were to lapse altogether. (" No, no," from the Deputy-Mayor). He did not expect that everyone would agree with him, but they would pass over that argument for the present. He thought that the proposal to exchange the license for a strip of land in Qeeen-street and ia fro et of the Lion Hotel was So trerneadously in favour of Messrs. Walker that he could not understand how the committee, which was composed largely of business men, should recommend such a one-sided pro- position. It would pay Messrs. Walker and Son to give the Corporation £3,000 to suppress the license in Bridge-street for the purpose of getting rid of the opposi- tion to the Lion Hotel. But when, in addition to that, they proposed to get rid of the license and sell it to the same people to be used in another part of the town for a strip of lAnd at the corner of Queen-street, which no arbitrator in the world would assess at anything like the vahie of the present premises, he thought the bargain was a monstrous one and monstrously in favour oi Meesrs. Walker. He did not know what the value of a license was. A great deal depended upen where it was placed ; a license might be worth anything up to £lO,OOO. It was proeosed to take the license from Bridge-street and transfer it, subj ect to the consent of the magistrates, to Orford-lane. it was true the Coun- cil was not the Licensing Committee, but they had a right to look at the ques-ion all round, and at all the possibilities which might arise in connection with the transfer ofethe liceese. He was in the district th At after- noon, and he found that whatever were the necessities of the district before, that since the granting of the license of the Hawthorn Inn, and the re-building of the premises, the dis:rict was more than sufficiently supplied alreedy,a.nd to put another license there,would bring about-- .

SOLDIERS KILLED.

A despatch from Walker, At-i-i-ne-s-ota, st Ites that a battle was fought on Wednesday morning thir:y miles from Vila place, between United States troops and Indians. A detachment 01100 men under General Bacon landed at Bagatanegeshirks Point. The Indians were not seen until eleven o'clock. Preparations for dinner were then going on. The solaiers were standing ia column when the first shot was fired from Bagahmege- shirk's Rouse. The bullet broke a man's arm. Then fire came from all directions. The soldiers charged, scattering the Inclans. Four soldiers wer killed and nine wounded. Reinforcements are being seat. NEW YORY,_ THURSDAY.

According t dvices receive! by the 'Wor'd" from Duluth, Genera! Bacon and al the regulars at Bear Lake have been massacrA. A regnest has been telegraphed to Washington for the des?atch of 5,000 troops. YELLOW FEVEII IN THE STATES.

div.head: TOWN ABANDONED TO STARVING NEGROES.
div.p: TOWN ABANDONED TO STARVING NEGROES.

A. telegram from Jacksm, slys the situa• tion is rapidly grlwinz or wirious. Most of the white population have atom:dined Jackson,leaving a thousand negroes surrounded by a cordon, who, owing t ) lack of provision for their maintenance, suffer from want of rood and medicines. The local railway traffic is practi- cally suspended, and the feeling in the infected section borders upon panic.

A LION-TAMER DECAPITATED-
TERRIBLE SCENE IN A CIRCUS.

A fearful tragedy is reported to have taken place at Norfolk, Virginia. During a performance given on Tuesday in a travelling Circus one of the principal items in the entertainment was t'ae entry of a tamer into a cage containing lions. Ile put the lions throagh a per- formance,and terminated it by pla,fing his bead in the mouth of one of the lions. On this occasion the lion closed his powerful jaws upon the man's neck anl bit the head off. Another lion became fr-nzied by the smell and sight of blood,and throwing itself upon the corpse a terrible fight ensued between the two lions for its pos. session. In the struggle between the infuriated beasts the body was torn to pieces. SHOCKING FATALITY AT HEYWOOD.

-- Yesterday morning a young man named Hugh Scott, of Heap Fold Farm, was driving a horse and lurry down a steep incline near h s home at Heap Bridge, Heywood, when the brake of the lurry broke He was unable to hold the horse, and he gat jammed between the lorry and a wall, receiving fright ul injuries. Death occurred /throat immediately. The deceased was well known,and wag only recently married. STABBING OUTRAGE AT SAN JUAN.
NEW Yon, THURSDAY._

A tragedy is recorted from San Juan,Puerto Rico. On Tuesday night there WM an agim ated discussion, fol- lowed by a scuffle in which a captain in the Puerto Rican Civil (heard wa 3 stabbed to death. The captain's conduct recently had been the subject of much adverse comment. _ _

div.head: RUNCORN YOU'ill DROWNED AT
div.p: A RUNCORN YOU'ill DROWNED AT
LATCIIFO
INQUEST AND VERDICT.

On Wednesday afternoon Mr. J. E. Wonley, coroner, held an inquast at the London and North-Western Hotet Runcorn, on the body of William Broady, aged 19, who was drowned in the Ship Canal at Latchford,on the 3rd inst.

William Broady, residing at 103 Shaw-street,Runcorn, said deeesta!d was his son. He was mate on the steam tug "Walton." He left home cn the 3rd inst, at 1.30 t 3 go to Warrington with the boat. Witness never saw him alive again. Samuel Banner, captain of the tug "Walton," stated that at 7.45 on the 3rd inst, he was tying up the boat at Twenty Steps Bridge, Latehford. The deoeased was in the act of putting a rope round the fist's timber head when he fell into the water. Thomas Bailey called out that th 3 man was in the water, and an attempt was made to reach the deceased with boat hooks. They called to witness to go after the deceased with the boat, and having unfastened it he proceeded towards deceased as quickly as possible. The deceased was drifting away from them, and he event- ually disapvared. If there had ben a man who was able to swim and dive they might have got hold of the deceased. It was very dark at the tin:ie.—The Coroner : Could not Bailey have thrown a life-buoy ?—Witn.ss Bailey was on his own flat. Everything was done that was thought of at the time. A shaft 17 feet 6ini would not reach the deceased. The life-buoys were on the top el the cabin. He thought the best thing to do was to move the boat towards the deceased and try to reach him, He could not have fetched a life-baoy, and moved the boat at the same time. If he had got a life-buoy and thrown it out it might have caught the deceased and kacked him unier the water. Thomas Bailey, 17, Princess-street, Runcorn, stated that he was on board tho fiat " Fannie," and saw the deceased fall into the water head first. Witness got a boat hook and tried to reach him. Toe hook dropped across the deceased's neck, but it was apparently upside down, and when he pulled in again it had not caught him. The deceased eventually disappeared altogether. D- eceased was not ia the water two minutes before he was drowned, The place was a very awkward one at night. —la reply to a Juror witness said he did not think de- ceased's head caught anything in the fall. Witness triel artificial respiration after the body was recovered, but it was of no avail. The body would be in the water 25 minutes. Witness could swim, but he was not in a fit state to ill SO, as he was troubled with a bad back. He had not the presence of mind to do So, as he thenght they could reacts the deceased with a boat hook. _

The Coroner said h 3 fund over and over again in holding inqaests on drowning cases, that if the deceaqed could hive swam ever so little his life would have been saved. It was a very curious thing to find that scarcely any of the men who got their living ant). spent their time on flats could swim the length of that tante. The jury returned a verdict to the effect that the deceased was" accidentally drowned."

div.head: LOCAL PROPERTY DISPUTE.
div.p: A LOCAL PROPERTY DISPUTE.

On Wednesday at St. Helens County Court,before his Honour Judge Shand, an action was heard in which Mrs. Temperance Taylor and Margaret Alice Shawcross, her sister, of Warrington, sued James Dickinson, of 108, Elephant-lane, Thatto Heath, to recaver possession of the house and premises in re. spect of which the previous application was made, and also £l7 for mesfie profits. Mr. Browne (War- rington) acted for plaintiffstand Mr.Crellin,of Black- burn,defended. Mr. Browne said the, property ori- ginally belonged to Richard Dickinson. After his death ,in 1.891,the property ultimately cams into the possession of the present defendant. The plaintiff s were the daughters of Richard Dickinson's eldest san. They were unaware of their title to the pro- perty, but immediately they learned it they laid claim to the property ; but defendant had refused absolutely to hand it over. That action was, there- fore, necessary to recover possession,—Mr. Crellin admitted the legal right of plaintiffs to the pro. perty,but said he had been unable to come to terms as to the atesne profits and the value of the im- provements defendant had made to the property...._ Mr. Browne offered to take £l2 as the ruesne pro- fits.—His Honour said he thought that reasonable. He thought plaintiffs ought t) allow defendant something for the erections he had put up in the rear of the premises.—Mr. Browne said he had no doubt his clients would allow something.—His Honour gave judgment for plaintiffs,to have posses- sion in seven clays, for £l2 mesne profits, and also judgment for plaintiffs on the set-off.

Joseph Burton solicitor, Runcorn, appeared for the complainant.— From the evidence it appeami that the parties were married on the Bth of July, 1833. There were three children of the marriage . Complainant had cause to complain of the cruelty and neglect of her husband. Even when sober he was not very kind, but when he Was drunk he was like a lunatic. As his conduct was such As was affecting her health, and on account of the threats he used towards her making her afraid of her life, she applied , to be allowed to live apart from him and to have the custody of the children. Since Whitsuntide she had receivel 75, 93, lls and 133 from h!m, but when hs was on the club she got 153 and 19s on different oacasions. —Mary Gibson, mother of the complainant, said that she , lived just across the street. She said "If you go. I will follow yota"She did so and tried to stop him from having the drink, and caught him by the throat Continuing, the defendant wound up a somewhat mixed statement, with confidently addressing the Chairman with "Between you and me, sir, all the bother is made through the moiher-in-h:w."—He hal no witness to call.—Mr. Burton submitted that the complainant would be content with 103 a week cad the Custody of the children if the application WAS granted. BAPTISMAL MEG ISSIEttAPION. Slr.—A little reftectioa on the part of your readers, will convince them, that toe empty boastings of your correspondents "C. 8. and " D.C." are s-anewhat previ- ous. The contreversy which has run 83 far away from the title at the head of th:s letter, was occasioned by a letter appearing in yoar iSSW3 of the 23rd July, signed "lons." This writer ventured the opinion, that the Raman Ca.ho in Doctrine of Baptismal Regeneration was founded on tradition. This opinion is knocked into the proverbial cocked hat by the teeowing " clear and intel- ligent" passages of the Wora of God. Christ said to His Apostles : "Go ye therefore and Mesh all nations,baptiz- ing them in the name of the Fativrtanl of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost " (Matthew xxviii. 19). Our Divine Lord furthermore rays, without any distinction what- . ver:"Except a man be born of water an I of the Spirit,he cannot enter into the Kingdom of God' (Johns iii.v). The words, especially if we take into consideration the force of the Greek text, in which this Gespel was writtea,in- chide all,without regard to age; and from them it can be rightly inferred that there is no ground for the assertion that adults alone can be baptized. Neither does the want of intention on the part of the infant, prove that infant baptism is invalid ; for as in the Jewish Church the faith of the parents or sponsors supplied the want 4f faith in the child in circumcision, so the want of faith in the child in baptism is supplied by the Church.Moreoverat is impossible for anyone who holds that we are born in original sin to call in question the necessity of infant baptism. Now the doctrine of original sin is an article of faith,for the scriptures teach that everyone is born in sin " Behold I was shapen in iniquity, and in sin did my mother conceive me." (Ps. U. 4). So necessary is the Sacrament to save all that St. Peter compares it to the ark : " The like figure where- unto even baptism do'.h also now save us." (I. Pater iii. 21). Baptism by immersion is nst necessary for we read (Acts eve 33) that St. Paul when in prison baptised hie jailor and famity,whicts ceruld not have been done by immersion,but either by pouring water on or sprinkling them. The sick and the imprisonel were accustamed to be beptised by either of these latter means(Neander,Vol. 1, p. 429). and were never afterwards re-bep- tised conditionally. In a subsequent issue of your much tried, and valuable paper, our geed friend "lona '' made the following very sen- sible remark : " The doctrines of Christianity are not based on speculations, however clever they may be, but upon clear and intelligible utterances of the Divine Word." The following explanation will prove beyond the shadow of a doubt that it is impossible to arrive at the " clear and ietslligible utterances of the Divine Word "by following the Protestant rule of faith. Pro- testants teach that we can only discover the true faith of Jesus by reading and interpreting for ourselves the Sacred Scrmturss. Catholics, while of course accepting the Famed Scriptures as the infallible word of God, accept also and equally as the infallible word of God the truths contained in Divine Tradition. By the truths of Divine Tradition we mean those artcles of faith which though not contained in the scriptures were nevertheless divinely revealed to the Apostles, and have been handed down by the living and infalliele voice of the Church. St. John gives the lesson why Tradition should be ad- mitted as a rule of faith. Be says : "There are also many other things which Jesus did, the which If they shculd be written everyone, I suppose that even the world itself could not contain the books which should be written." (John :xi. 25). Let it be remembered that St. John is the last of the Evangelista, acd,with three other Gospels before his mind.makes this statement, and it will follow that the four Gospels give but an incomplete epitome of our Saviour's discourses and miracles. The Sacred Epistles scarcely dwell on either. We must look to tradition or the unwritten word for a fuller explanation of our hely faith, and we are warranted in doing so by the exhortations of St. Paul: 'The things which thou hart heard of me, among many witnesses, the same commit thou to faithful nien, who shall be able to teach others also." (2 Tien. 11. 15). " Steed fast and hold the traditions which ye have been taught. whether by word or our E;:estlei " (2. These. 11. 15). Protestants must trust to t edition for a fuller ex- planation tlthe Blessed Trinity and of the mystery of the Incarnation, or of the procession of the Holy Ghost, than is given in the Sacred Scriptures. Where is their scriptural authority for changing the Sabbato to Sunday ? Tradition is most use- ful in settling disputel points of doctrine. The following facts prove the Protestant rule of faitb,or private interpretation of the scriptures to be untenable. Such a rule of faith could not have been adopted by Christians before the art of printing was invented,that is for fifteen centuries,for during that period copies of the sacred scriptures could only be obtained in manuscript. and at enormous cost. It must strike every Protestant who carefully studies the sacred scriptures, that our Saviour, neither directly nor indirectly,foretold that the New Testament should he written, and, after the death of the Apostles, form the Christians' sole guide of faith ; whilst on the other hand, He insists on the Divine authority of the Church. If private interpreta- tion ot the scriptures be necessary to gain a knowledge of the true faith, how are the ignorant and unlettered in the present time to be in- structed in the true. religion ? Private internretetion of the Word of God was never allowed in the 011 Testa- ment, but the people looked up to the priests as their teachers in religion. This will be seen by consulting : "Amariah, the chief priest, is over you in all matters of the Lord." (2 Chronicles xix. ii). The priests are com- manded to teach the children of Israel all the statutes which the Lord hath spoken unto them by the hand of Moses." (Lev. x. ii). The priesiei of the new law hole the same authority in Christ's Church,as is evident from Christa' words : —Go ye therefore and teach all nations baptising them in the came of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost." (Matt. xxviii. 19). All who refuse to obey their teaching are to be regarded: "As an heathen man and a publican " (Matt. xviii, 17). The faithful are warned that no prophecy or exposition of Scripture is of private interpretation. 'No prophecy of Scripture is of any priva'e interpretation " (2 Peter i 20)." For the prophecy came not in the old time by the will of man, but holy men Of Ged spake as they were moved by the Holy Ghost "(2 Peter i. 20). Tens faith requires us to believe without doubting what Christ has revealed. And we can only know what Christ has revealed on the testimony and authority of the Catholic Church which Christ appointed to teach all nations. May not we Catholics, truly,raise up our hearts (Sursum Corda),and thank our good God, that we are in the barque of Peter, out of which Christ calms the tempest, and stills the waves. Deo Gratias.—Yours, SUBSUM GORDA.

P.S.—I notice a long string of objections made by your correspondent C.B. He demands in the most per- emptory manner an answer to each of his objections,— which by the way are, in the main, copied from the notoriously dishonest writer Littledale, saying " I give chapter and verse." Now this is exactly whac he fails to do. Any of your readers who cares to look at the charges will find them s- t down somewhat in this form : Bellarrnine says so and so : Labbe and Cosssrt say this and that : but no reference is given either of book or page. It does not teem to occur to this reckless writer, that it would take about six weeks to search out the refutation of a calumny supposed to have its origin in the works of these great writere. Scatemente made with- out reference are not worthy of notice. The charges made by C.B. against individual popes even if true (which I do not admiP) do not tell against the dogma of Infallibility does not mean that the Pope is impeccable or especially exemot fr•rn liability to sin. The Popes have been inde,d, with few exceptions. men of virtuous lives. Many of them are honoured as martyrs. Seventy-nine art invoked on our altars. as Saints eminent for their laoliassi. Thl avowed enemies if the Church charge only five or six Popes with immorality. Than, even admitting the truth of the accusations brought avainst thm, w 3 have foitit-thres virtuous to one bad Pope, while there was a Judas Iscariot among the twelve Apostles. There was a Salaam among the Propheta,and Csiphas among the High Priests: of the old Law.—S.C. [Correspondence on this subject must new cease.— EDITOR " Examiner."]

div.head: EARLESTO WN AND NEWTON.
div.p: EARLESTO WN AND NEWTON.
Poracz Clam.

At the Police Station, Earlestown, on Tuesday I morning before Mr. J. W. Emmett, William Woods. was charged with being drunk on Monday, and was fined 23 61 and costs. 1.0.G.T. HoPE o EARLESTOWN LODGE. At the meeting on Monday Bro. J. Singleton pre- sided over a god attendance. Several candidates joined. Arrangements were made for the forthcom- ing 26th anniversary,which is to be held on the 22nd 23rd and 24th. A paper was then read by Bro. G. Clarke, D.E.Supt. on" Notes of encouragement to Temperance Workers," which was of a very inter- esting character and dealt with what had been done since the Order was introduced into Earles- town in Octabar 1872. Bro. J.Woods moved a vote of thanks,seconded by Bro. Webster. There was a good discussion. CONGREGATIONAL CHURCH, NEWTON. I -

On Sunday afternoon,a musical service was given in the above church, in support of the choir funds. The selection submitted was the cantata " The Angel of the Harvest," the whole of the choruses being given in a very able and efficient manner by the choir,under the leadership ot Mr. A. Knight,who presided at the organ. The soloists were Miss Mather, " The reapers chant their joyful lays ;" Miss Corlett " From living creations far and near;" Mr. Pennington" Nature in great diapason ;" Mr.O. Kidd" Ye sons of labour." There was a fair audi- ence, and the service altogether was of a most suc- cessful character.

EARLESTOWN ORCHESTRAL SOCIETY. This excellent musical society opened their season on Saturday by a social evening in the Town Hall, Earlestown. There were about 100 persons present and the band,under the conductorship of Mr. Ashley rendered some excellent selections of music for dancing. Messrs. W. Monks and Joseph Banton officiated as M.C's and the whole arrangements were carried out under the supervision of Mr. James Sad- worth. The catering for the inner man was very efficiently undertaken by Mrs. Gutheridge and gave the utmost ss.tisfaction. The proceeds were in aid ofathe band fund.

div.head: GOOD TEMPLARY.
div.p: GOOD TEMPLARY.

The South-West -1-4tneLhire Di trict Council of the Juvenile Order was held on Saturday at Stub- thaw Cross. Ashton. Bra. E. Ne.vnian, D.5.1.T., reported 2,053 members in 31 Temples; 20 had entered the Adult Order; one new Temple had been open, and others had arranged soon to open. There was an increase of 75 members on the quarter. The Temples hid arranged for extra work for the coming Annual Competitive Examinations next session to be held at Liverpool. An address was given by Bro. F. W. Hall, aud after tea a public meeting was held. The Chairman was the D.5.1.T., Bro. E. Newman, and the speaker Bro. F W. Hall. Songs, recita- tions, &c., were nicely rendered by friends of Ash- ton

VIADUCT INSTITUT/4 BOWLING CLUB, ELILLESTOWN. The season in connection with the above club, was brought to a clo-e on Saturday afternoon, in brilliant weather. The greens were ire splendid conditiou, and there was consequently a large mus- ter of members. Sides were chosen by the Captains Messrs. Clough and Mather, and after some very interesting mains, Mr. dough's team proved 'v ictorio us. All the players afterwards adjourned to the Viaduct Hotel,where a substantial knife and fork tea was partaken of, and thoroughly enjoyed. The subsequent proceedings were conducted in a convivial manner,several toasts being proposed and honoured in the customary way. 'the harmony was ably sustained by Messrs. div.p: THE DANCING-ROOM QUESTION AT ST. HELENS.

Henry Roberts, a fore—man in the mplay of tle S. Helens Corporation, and living at 29, Vincent-street,was charged at the Police Coutt on Monday with keeping and using a room in Sharp-street for public mudc and danc- ing without a license. After hearing the evidence, the bench said there had clearly been a breach of the law, and Roterts was fined Ll and Bs. 6.1. costs. LORD STANLEY AT ST. HELENS.

The Mali lust Schools, Sutton, St. Helens, were form- ally opened on Saturday afternoon by Lord Stanley, M.P., who said that nothing c mid be a better subj-sct of congratulation than when, as in this case, through the efforts of the people themselves, the lives and education of thoe who came after them were t) be better looked after. Sir El ward Russ•ll remarked that of late veers in this country they could all bear testimony that educa- tion, which formerly was considered oily a matter for the higher cl sses, was bccmniog one in which all per- sons were interested. DEATH OF Ma. SHARP, OF Sr. ITELENS. Much regret has boon occasioned in S. Helens by Vie death of Mr. Thomas Shrrp, of the [follies, Rainford road, which took p!ace on Saturday afternoon, after a short illness. Mr. Sharp was the son of a well-known St. Helens man, and had been a book-keeper at tLe effi-ies of Messrs. Grcenall, Whitley. an i Co. or ahout twenty years, having previously been a clerk at the British Plate Glass Work4,Ravenhead. He had been in delicate health for some time, but had only been ill a week prior t) his death. Mr. Sharp was 51 years of age, and was a prominent sw.mber of the Congr gational Church, be the members of which and a large circle of friends he. was greatly respected. The funeral took place at St. Heins Ceme•ory on Tuesday. REMARKABLE PROPERTY DISETTE AT ST. HELENS. At St. Helena County Court oa Wednesday Mr. A. Browne, of Warrington, applied to his Honour Judge Shand for the appointment under the Settled Lands Acts of a trustee for the purpose of sale of cottage land and premises at Thatto Heat's, St. ffe!ens—His Honour doubted whether he had power to appoint the trustee without also making an order for the money to he brought into court, as one nf the plaintiffs, although married, was a minor.—Mr.Browne asked that the order to made without having the =nay brought into court. The costs of such proceedings were enormous. He had a case of the same kind at Warrington, where the value of the property was £9B, and they had to pay £32 costs to get the money out of court--His Honour said he was astounded at that statement. After further consideration ha made an order appointing a trustee to sell.

div.head: --- SWIMMING GALA. AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: --- SWIMMING GALA. AT WARRINGTON.
THE L0.7,A1, CHAMPIONSHIPS.

The concluding gala of the season T. 9.19 held at the Corporation BIGnA, Warrington, on Tuesday eveolng. 'There was a fair atteod Ince and an unusually interesl- ing programme was submi:ted. The Mayo: (Aldsrman J. E. Wright) prfsidei. The officials were : Judges, Messrs. J. Critchley, John Evans, and T. Locker ; com- petitors' stewards, Massrs. R. T. Harding, and C. H. Wood ; check starter. Mr. G. Grounds ; timekeepers' Messrs. Gittens and Burrows. It is rather surprising that the attendance was only mldiocre when oae talos into cons:deratiou the events wnich wEra brought off, and which included the schoolboy championship of War- rington and the amateur Cha.npionship of Warrington and district. MREBERS 50 YARDS HANDICAP.

Abont thirty members turned out for this race, and some cieetal swimming took place. (he first in each heat, of which there were six, were elieible to swim in the final. When Robertson made his appsarance for his heat, w rich was his first appearaece in public since his his attainment of the In'ernational cap, he was r.sceived With prolonged cheers. The following won their heats : A. Baker and A. Newton (dead heat), A Furness, J. E. Crtchley, J. Hughes. J. Cronshaw, and B. Hayward. The race for the final was well contested. Biker, 2nd prize, silver cigarette case ; A. Furnese, 3rd prize, sleeve links and studs ; andJ. Flughes, 4te peze, clock ; J. Crenshaw, 511 was allowed a consolation prize. - " THORNTON " CHALLENGE COWL. Toe competition for the possessiou for twelve months of the challenge bewl and which carries with it the schoolb my championship of Warrington and District was one of intense interest to the youngsters. The race was For 50 yards—two lengths—the previoae holder being C. Turner, the son of Mr. Fair Turner the well-known athlete. There were six entrants and their names were as toliows : T. Broadhurst, People's College ; C Turner, ' Heath Side ; W Broadaurst, People's College ; H ing, Silver-street ' • J Ashton, People's College ; and F Reteerts, Heath Side. All turned out for the race ; the winner was C Turner, who swam with a beautiful and clean side stroke which evoke] universal admiration. He covered the required distance with plenty to spare, the time being 41 seconds. If the time is compared with the final of the memeers' race whin wan 44 1 5 seconds, it will be seen that you e Turner is a most promising swimmee The result of the race was C Turner, let prize, sileer challenge hew!, (presented by Mr. H. Thernton) and ged centre medal ; F Broaihurst 2nd prize, silver medal; and W Broa llourst, 3:d prize, brenze medal. LICENSED VICTDALLERS' CHALLENGE TROPHY. This was the event which created most interest, amongst the older swimmers. The competition was for the silver chalenge shield Redlich carries with it the amateur championship of Warrington and district, the previous holder being Mr. T. Locker. The following were the comp-eitors : A isleton, T Davies, P Furness, WCr iehton, W Ashton, and A G Robertson. The race, which was for 150 yards (six lengths), was a close one thouzh two gave up early in the race. The result was: VVCreiehton, let priza, silver challenrrA elsield and eeld tn-rial; T Davies, 2nd prize, gold meda'; W Ashton, 3rd prize, gold centre medal. THE CHAIRMAN'S emeness. The MAYOR (Aldermen J. E. Wright) in a few well- chosen woris expressed the pleasure it gave him to be preseet that eeening. He most heartily congratulated the Warrington Swimming Chat) on the work they were doing. He would be only too pleased to help them in every way to make their object successful. He thought their thanks were particularly due to Mr. Henry Thorn- ton and other gent'emen who had helped so generously. (Appl, me.)

SHOCKING REVELATIONS.

On Monday morning at the Warrington Borough Police Court two cases were heard in which Inspector McAteer, of the N.S.P.C.C., was the prosecutor. Mr. Birchall occupied the,chair, and there were also on the Bench Alderman Blacklaurat, Councillors Shaw Green and Smethurst.

Thomas and Margaret Potter, 38, Glazebrook-street, were charged with neglecting their child Nellie, aged 11, la a mauler likely to cause unnecessary suffering and and injury to health. Inspector McAteer stated that on the 21st of last month he wen: ts the Fairfield School and saw the child. He examined lir iu the presence of the school-mistress, and found her to be in a filthy condition,especially about the head, which was covered with a mass of sores. He took the child home. Subsequently he took the child to Dr. Bowden'e surgery, and the doctor examined her. The child was in a terrible state. The case should have come before the court a week ago, but the female defers. dant was then in gaol, and tho hearing was adjourned. He (the inspector) had made several inquiries respecting the man, and found that he bore a good character. The woman's character was not at all satisfactory. Drink was at the bottom of it all. Sergeant Lewis gave cora...donative evidence. Dr. Bowden stated that ha examined the child's head, and found more than half the scalp covered with scabs, simply brought about by an accumulation of discharge from scores o a the head. It was want of cleanliness which had brought about the child's conditien.—laspec- tor McAteer : Was the child suffering unnecessary pain? —Dr. Bowden: The child complained that she could not sleep or ett,as her head was itching and burning. Toe female defendant said it was nothing but a skin disease.

Mrs Aires, 20, Craszebr avk street, :aid she had had the chid five we k, The child had been badly treated and neglected. Mrs. Potter said she had done her best for the child, and she could do no more. She was not to lo:ame but her husband was.
The male defeadant said he had worked at the Ceiw- tery for 19 years aud his wife had always had hie wages at the week end. _
Two neighblurs name I Mrs. M)lyneux and Mrs. Houghton and Councidor Evans gave toe defendant an excellent c'narac.er.

Mrs Potter : I have be3h a bstter molher to his child than he kits be3o a father to mine. The cage a4atast tile male defoadant was dismissed and the female defendant was committed to gaol for fourteen days without the option of a lin3.

Reuben Worrall and Miry Jane Worrall, 9, Morris- court, were summoned for neglecting their four children. The Caee had been adjouraed frora a month previous. Inspector McAteer said when the case was befora the coact on the 2nd of last month the magistrates ad. jiurned it in order Co sea whether defendants would effect an improvement. s was sorry t 3 say that the aijournment bad been no go He hart called at the house on two or thsee different occasions, and it was in the same condition as when he first visited it.—Urs. Worrell : Have no we bought a new bed and a new set of belsteads,as wed as clothes for the children ?—Wit- ness : It has ben since the 28th of last month.—Mrs, Worrall : It is more poverty than neglect. The mile defendant said he was not baking now, though that was his trade. de was labouring. P.C. Monks said he visited the house on the 24th of lugust and saw Mrs. Worrall ant the two children Joseph and Maud. They were both very dirty, the girl being, if anything, in a worse condition than the boy. Oa going upstairs no saw an old mattr:si, upon which the two eldest boys slept. There was no co7ering. In another corner there was a broken badsteid, the bedding was c3vered with filth.
--- The Chairman : S noply ag bad as pigs. Pigs can only Sleep in their own filth. Mrs. Worroll : Tuei pot me down worse than I am.

P.C. Dawson gave c'oiroboretive evidence. Toe male defendant said he had been out of work f tea weeks, and they hid to sell tieir house up. Th..y hal before that a good lause of f urniture. The Ch . Tha;:s no reason why you should be dirty. Sip is not dear. Defendant : The house is not dirty. _

Toe Chairman : You h Iva hear the evidence. You and the children are lying in filth like pigs. L hat is not dirty ydur notion of filth it very strange. Mr. %torrid : I don't see why we should b 3 prose- cuted. The house is clean.

Councilbr Smethurst, Superintendent Monaghan, and P.C. Monks left the court to visit the house and upon their return Superintendent Monaghan haid that in tie kitchen were three chairs and a wooden box. The place was not very clean. In the float bedroom there was an iron bedstead, and aa old tick and mattress. There ap- peared to be no c evering except an old overcoat. There was a svooclea bedstead with a tick on it in the back room, but no bed coverin;:. The I aipector : The bedstead has beeh put in the house since the 28:h September. Coanciller Smethurst also described the house. When they opeaed ths door the officer said there had been an improvement. Inspector McAteer : I stand by what I have said. Oa the 28th there was no alteration. . . .

The Chairman said the majority of the magistrates were inclined to give defendants another chance. The case would bs adjourned for a month,during which time thy wou'd expect a substtniqal improvement.

div.p: , UNIVERSITY EXThAbIUN LECTURES AT WARRINGTON.

There was an encouraging attendance at the first of the course of six lectures on the instory of the English people (1514 to 1689) whica was delivered in the Co-operative Hall, Sankey-street, ou Wednesday even lug. Mr. W. lir. tie Bargee, M.A., Oxford, was the lee- ' turer, and his subjeee wes " The Reformation in England." Ia the eriaeace of Mr. F. W. Monks, the lecturer was introduced Pet the Rev. Morley Stevenson. 1 lii pel Luning this duty, Mr. Stevenson said they all regretted the absence pi Der. F. W. Peones, tee president of the committee, who ought to have taken the ctiair. Mtn regard to tile course oi lectures he could remember a good mans/courses of University Extension lectures in Warringtoa ; some had been extremely succeseful and others he regretted to say had been wee reverse. It was some little tune since they had a course ot cruse lectures and the committee had been somewhat anxious for time success at toe Course which began enat evening. lie had come to tniuk that the minus or success of inch a coorse depended upon the subject being attractive and interesting, and also upon tne lecturer who dealt with the subject. Trio subject before them Was an nistoricel one, ani tiley Ought to ue, it they wre not, interested in tne history at their own country. It was the past which had made ttie Engliela nation wnat it was at the present time, and it rested with the present' generation to mitre tne English nation what it suauld be the tutare. As ragereeti the lecturer he could not say mach in his presence, Out the Committee bad every reason to believe from wear cney based from outer places that in ilea they had a lecturer who would interest and charm teem, and make his lectures attractive as well as useful. lie would now ask Mr. Lie Baran to deliver his lecture, (Applause). the LECTURER at the outset explained the system adopted at the lectures. Auer the delivery of the lec- ture a CissS was held aud papers oa tile suoject of tee Lecture weie invited. TWSiu he a,terwards examined and comm uted upon. the history of Euglaed, ne said, was the hetery oh the development of the Eaglisia people. He wished to linpress upon Guam time grew. Ilistur.Cai pcincipte that events in nistory Gnat had happened in nay given age or century must be traced beck to their begieuings mu time past and ttazeill as far as they could onward to their results in tti LUCLIre. 'fbe ()eject oh tee present course of lectures was not to give a complete re- cord of all the impertaet events that trapuespvirleeicoduultd- ing the tune Out to tiace the most eiguitheaat incidents in tee lite and character of the English i people. Tee history of the development of time Euejistt ,be divided nue three great epochs. First, there was the waking ut tue great ELiglian pzuple. Rome was not built in a day and time making of Vac English Peeple took a thousaud yeare. From time day when ch., great Anglo- Saxons lauded at Stites Fleet in 419 a thousand years elapsed eje at the conclusion o the wars ot the Roses and the accession of Henry VII. 1485, the • English people could be pro- nounced a united people. It was not till than that they became a nation that felt conscious of unity and a common patriotism. Auother of the great epochs in English hietery Was" modern England" which dated 1 from the revolution of 1689. Parliamentary institutions, cabinet government and all the present forms of politic at life had been mouldee to their present shape in these last two centuries. The third great period in English history was that whieli commenced with tee ace-seion of Henry VII and concluded with the expulsion of Tames ll—the period of the Tudor and Stuart sovereigns. Tbis was a time of etrugele and war. Tele lecturer proesedeci to give a graphic description of the state of Europe in toe sixteenth century; the age of conflict between the old order and the new. Tile new order was the revival learning an.i the Reformation—euthusiaLm for intellec- tual progress and moral reform. Pee chief in- cidents in the Eneliah Reformation were described as well as the policy oh the Tudor monarchy. The Tudor sovereigns, imperious in character, were animated by , political rather than by religious aim 4 ; they were swerehns of cutters and &relish to the backbone. They were resolved to make themselves great and the English people great too. The zeta which led up to and resulted in the:religious compromise in England were related,and the lecturer showed how the revolt from Papal supre- macy constituted the first stage in the asseitton by the English people of their national unity. A tribute to the great work of Eliz tbeth in uniting the English people was paid by the lecturer, and he concluded by asking his hearers to remember that there ir as a continuous enuaretion running through the whole course of national life, and that all that had happened, that interestd us, arid was of importance to us, had its beginnings far beck in the remote ages that were gone.
