RUGBY FOOTBALL. Another Saturday has gene by and wills it an ,t'oer I couple of points in the Lancashire League. At pi esent Warrington are in excessively poor point-capturing forre,and look like having a bad season iinless the team , has a sudden acquisition of strength. That Expensive combination,the Salford fifteen, were Warrington's con- querors on Saturday. The adverse score was the usual one of three tries,though the visitors dil show some im- provement by notching a try and escaping the indignity lof being pilled. It is rather curious that the three clubs who have defeated Warrington Oldham, Widnes, and Salford, have each scored nine points, and in two instances against nothing by Warrington. There is some slight consola- tion in the fact that Warrington's opponents have so far been, in fur out of the five matches, the strongest teams in the League. With the exception of Br .uzhton Rangers, there is no club lett which Warrington have not met up to now and have any particular reason to fear. There are several as good, or as bad as Warrington, but beyond the top six, none betty. There should therefore be better times in store, e592c ally when the" new man" come.

Both " Old Sol " and Pilllisting were present at New Barns on Saturday, in company with about 10,000 sup- porters of the Beds. " Old Sol" beamed warmly on the multitude, and assisted in steaming a lot of Turkey red cat of the Salford players' jerseys. These self-same jerseys are very nice to look ac—when their wearers are cool—but when the polyglot team gets full steam up they decidedly lose caste as well as colour. Some of the per- spiring Welshmen absorbed such a large quantity of Turkey red into their plump anatomies that it is possible the Salford C anamittee may shortly be relieved of the necessity for providing jerseys at all. Nature's original covering, and the colouring combined, will amply suffice to clothe the representatives ot the Royal Borough in the requisite red.

I should think there were nearly twice as many sPec- tators on Saturday as at the similar encounter a year ago. Salford' a successes of last season and this,have re- tinted in a large increase in the "ga :es." Ten thousand is quite an average crowd at New Barns, while the total rises to neirer twenty thousand when Oldham and Swinton visit the Royal Borough. Salford's little swachP —that Slough of Despond which used to pave" the way to the vround—bag decreased as rapidly' as the club's prosperity has increased, but it is not quite gone. There are still om or two fairly commodious puddles, though there is dry land betwem, and at one time there was not. Salford is to be blessed with a county match this season, and ere then the roadway to the field has to be placed in through good erder.

Thoug.h Salford obtained a fairly easy victory, th was not much disparity bstweea the two teams. Oa paper the difference seemed immense, for the bomesters had their full team out, with the exception of noskins. and as far as names go there can be no comparison between the players in each team. But Salford are not playing at all well just now. They have got toe men, but the combination between them is very far from being perfect. Taking the game as it was played on Saturday, I think had IVarrington possessed a back or two with a turn of speed they would not have found it difficult ts win. They had more opportunities to score than the winners, and presmted a bettPr defence. It was slowness, principdly, that lost the game for the visitors. Salford had the speed an iit was well utilised when an opening was found.

Up to half-time the most sanguine suppoit?r of the Reds could not have been confident of his team's success, as tho scores were equal at the Interval, and Wars-in:ton had show', up well. In fact they were the first to score, and caused an alteration of the scoring board before the game was five minutes old. "Smack" caught his oppon- ents napping and tricked them beautifuly,finally giving Moores an easy chance, which that usually s sfe player mulled. Still the Warrinton skipper's skilful play had carried the game well into no home htlf. From the next scrimmage amends were made by Moores, who darted in after remivarz a well-judged pass from Bate. Encouraged by this early success Warriogton fairly made tho pace a hot one,and Salford were herd put to it to defend their line. For a quarter of an hour they were completely "bottled-up," but al', last the seige was raised ad Warrington were forced to a lopt defensive tacttcs. It was not long before the homesters equalised. Politics got over after some hap-haz trd piecing and at half-time the teams cried quits.

Th 9 second moiety opsued quite as sensationally, but not so satisfactorily from a Warrington point of vie-v,as the first. Moores failed to return the ball from the k;ck and the homesters scrimmaged near the Warrington line. A couple of sharp exchanges between Grey and Thomas gave Miles possession,and the wing man dashed in at the corrpr. A spasmodic effort at retaliacion on Warrington's part was a.l that intervene] between this incident and its repetition. Exactly the same tactics were adapted and the same remit followed, SAlf,r I at threequart,r time leading by three tries to one. Towards the c'oie Warringtoa livened up,and a °maple of chances went begging after Bate made goad openings. A furtlvr score seemed inevitable when inexorable "time " caused a cessation of hostilities and awarded t le victory to Sal. I kid.

On the winning side, Gray, Pearson and Miles were the most prominent among the backs. Perm-was especially active and needed far more watching than any other man in th 3 team. Tom Williams Was in rather poor form, and Smith was little better. The for- 'wards are a fine, well-drilled lot, and w r 3 ably lei by Gledhill, Moss, and Fisher. " Smack " Sate played one of his very best games, wad all Warrington people know what that means. He was far and away superior to the Salford pair, who are by no means" muffs" at the game. Ashurst supported him well, and the threequarters all did as well as could be expected, though they were undoubtedly weak as an attacking force.- Hallam who made his debut as fullback for the first time shaped exceedingly well. He WAS rather too sager at times, but made no serious mistake, while his punting WSS all along marked by power and judgment. I think he will make a good man for the p)si-ion it he learns to keep cool.

The County trial match on Wednesday afternoon pro- vided an interesting game, though it did not attract very many spectttors. Scori, g was rather prolific, the Protables registering 13 points against 10 points for the Possibles. Though seven points behind at half Lime the winners pulled up well in the second half and had the best of the game. Undoubtedly the finest threequarter on the day's play was Traynor (St. Helens), wh ) played a sterling game right thnugh. Valentine was plainly saving himself for Swinton's important matCh with Salford to-day (S iturday), and the same might be slid of one or two other pltyers. Of the junior exponents given a trial, Altham of Morecambe showed very fair form, but Duck, of Broughton was a failure. There were several important absent3es, inc!uiing J. T. Bats (War- rington), and this was one reason why the selection of the County team to oppose Cheshire, at Stockport, on Saturday nest took such a long time. Finally ths fol- lowing were chosen :—Batey (Widnes), back; Valentine (Swinton), Traynor (St. Helena), S. Lees (Oldham), and Martin (Oldham), three-quart)r backs ; Pearson (Swin- ton) and Griffiths (Salford), half backe ; Hampsou (Widnes), Evans (Swinton), Steel (Broughton Rarsers), Briers (St. Helens), Williams (Salford), Moffat (o.doam), Whitehead (Broughton Rangers), and Johns° 1 (Swinton). forwards. Reserves : Thomas (Oldham), back ; Badger (Swinton), and Ho,kios (Salford), thres-quarter baelts ; Lawton (Gcloarn), half back ; Tayhr (I.!,igh), Worthing- ton (Tyldesley), and Heslop (Widnes), forwards.
Warrington are with,u; a single representative. Wit 3 ks Li p 1 re through failMg to play in the trial game, while 'Parlor did no show good enough form to justify his selection.

A. It or CUNNINGHAM'S HIGH-CLASS ISINSRAL WATRRS —Advt. DEATIE OF A CANINE FAVOURITE. OA Saturday a railway lorry ran over a dog which had to be subsequently shot. The dog which was a collie named Shep, belonged to Mr. James Ashley, farmer, Wash-lane, Latchford, but better known as the faithful attendant on the mem- bers of the Warrington police force, for the last 7 years or so. The doglknew the beats, and was very familiar with every officer, though he had his favourites.On several cccasions the nominal fine of 2s 6.1 has been paid by members of the force, as he was averse to having a muzzle on. He has na- ttered aid to the police force on many occasions, and many a " rowdy" has been suddenly sobered by Shep's interference as a maintainer of law and order. more. Mr. A. Semen was highly applauded for his siag- ing of the "Village Blacksmith" and the " Day of Rest," while Mr. Corrin's Eon " IYr:ea the tide comes in " waS also executed in masterly style.
